samples.result:
# The Hours Nobody Claims

There is a particular quality to the light in a hospital waiting room at three in the morning. I don't mean the fluorescent hum of it, though that is part of it—the way the tubes buzz at a frequency just below hearing, the way they turn every surface the color of old teeth. I mean something about the light itself, as if it has traveled further to get there, as if it is tired. The vending machine glows like an altar. The linoleum stretches out in its repeating pattern of gray and grayer, and somewhere down the corridor a door opens and closes with a sound like a book shutting.

I have spent more nights than I can count in rooms like that one. Not as a patient, usually. As the person in the chair. The one holding the coat, the purse, the phone with its dying battery. The one who has volunteered to wait so that someone else can pace, or pray, or fall apart in private. And I have come to believe that these hours—the hours nobody claims, the hours that belong to the waiting—teach us something that the bright hours cannot.

---

The world at three in the morning is a draft of the world. The final version hasn't arrived yet. The streets outside are empty in a way that feels less like absence and more like held breath. Even the architecture seems different: the buildings that looked solid and indifferent by daylight now look like they are dreaming. Their windows are dark eyes. Their fire escapes cast shadows that don't match anything. A traffic light cycles from red to green for no one, dutiful and absurd, a sentry saluting an empty square.

I used to think that night was simply the absence of day, the way silence is the absence of sound. I don't think that anymore. Night is its own country. It has its own physics, its own etiquette, its own population. The people you meet at three in the morning—nurses coming off shift, taxi drivers between fares, the woman walking three dogs that may or may not be hers, the kid behind the gas station counter watching something on a cracked phone—are citizens of that country. They carry themselves differently. There is a recognition that passes between them, slight as a nod across a train platform, that says: *you are awake in the wrong direction, too.*

My grandmother used to say that the hours after midnight belonged to the dead, and she meant it half as superstition and half as observation. She grew up in a house where someone was always dying—the usual parade of consumption and failed hearts and accidents with farm machinery that filled the parish records of her generation—and she learned early that grief keeps rural hours. It does not wait for business days. It does not observe the weekend. It arrives when it arrives, and the living must make tea at two in the morning and sit with it.

I think about her often when I am awake in the small hours. Not with sadness, exactly. With something closer to professional respect. She knew how to wait. She knew how to keep a vigil. These are dying arts, and I don't mean that as a pun. We have engineered so much waiting out of our lives— instant everything, same-day everything, the eradication of the pause—and we have not replaced the thing the waiting was for. The waiting was not wasted time. The waiting was where the mind went to do its slow, unsupervised work. It was where the unspeakable got spoken to oneself. It was the antechamber.

---

There is a kind of thinking that only happens when you are too tired to lie to yourself. I discovered this in a surgical waiting room seven years ago, during the eleven hours my father was on a table having a part of him removed that the surgeons kept referring to, with a cheerfulness that I have never quite forgiven, as "thebits that don't matter." Nothing in the body is a bit that doesn't matter. I knew that then and I know it now, and at hour six of that waiting I also knew every other thing I had spent a lifetime not knowing. I knew that I had been cruel in ways I had filed under honesty. I knew that I had been a stranger to people I claimed to love because strangeness was easier. I knew that my father, who was at that moment opened up like a letter under a blade, had spent his whole life trying to tell me something and that I had never once asked him to finish the sentence.

The vending machine offered me a chocolate bar that tasted like drywall. I ate it without pleasure. Down the hall, a family I did not know received news I will not describe, and the sound they made was a sound I hope never to hear again and will never forget. A nurse came out eventually and said my father was doing better than expected, using the tone of someone reporting a slight improvement in the weather, and I understood that she had said this sentence ten thousand times and that it was both true and insufficient, and that she knew that, and that she said it anyway because it was what there was to say.

What do you do with that kind of knowledge? You cannot keep it. It is too large for the day. You fold it up small and put it in the pocket of the daylight self, and most days you forget it is there. But some nights it presses against you like a stone in a shoe, and you get up, and you make tea, and you sit with it, the way my grandmother sat with the dying and the waiting. And if you are lucky, you learn to stop apologizing to yourself for being awake.

---

Insomnia is a badly named condition. It sounds like a simple deficit, a sleep-shaped hole in a person. But anyone who has lived with it knows it is not an absence. It is a presence. It is a second life, lived in parallel, with its own weather and its own logic. The insomniac becomes a scholar of her own ceiling, an expert in the specific gravity of four a.m., a naturalist of the sounds a house makes when it thinks no one is listening. The boiler's decision. The refrigerator's long apostrophe. The neighbor's television muttering through the wall like a guilty conscience.

I have a friend who spent a decade unable to sleep and who told me, once, that the worst part was not the tiredness. The tiredness became ordinary, a background radiation. The worst part was the loneliness of it—the sense of being the only person in the building, the only person in the city, the only person in the history of the world who was awake and thinking and afraid. I told her that this was not true, that the world has always been full of the sleepless, that whole industries and religions and poems have been built by people at three in the morning, but she looked at me with such a flat and loving pity that I understood I had said the wrong thing. It does not help the insomniac to know that others have suffered. The night is not a community. The night is a series of sealed rooms.

What helped her, she said, was giving up the fight. Not surrendering to despair—she had done plenty of that—but surrendering to the hours themselves. She started getting up. She made elaborate breakfasts at four. She read books that required a patience daylight had never afforded her. She wrote letters. She learned, in other words, to treat the sleepless night not as a theft but as an inheritance: strange property, poorly lit, but hers.

---

I walk at night when I cannot sleep, and I have come to love the city in its undress. The city at night is a city that has taken off its makeup. You can see the infrastructure of its vanity: the scaffolding, the sodium stain of streetlights on wet pavement, the delivery trucks idling like patient animals, the steam rising from grates with a theatricality that daylight would render embarrassing. The city at night is honest about its plumbing. It is honest about its bones.

And the people in it—the night people—are honest in a way that day people are not. The man at the twenty-four-hour laundromat folding his shirts with the concentration of a monk. The women coming out of the club at closing, their makeup irretrievable, their laughter too loud and too real. The old man feeding pigeons at a bus stop at an hour when no bus will come, because the pigeons are hungry and he is awake and the two facts have found each other. There is a tenderness in these encounters that daylight forbids. You can talk to a stranger at three in the morning in a way you cannot talk to a stranger at noon. The noon stranger will think you want something. The three a.m. stranger knows you want nothing that can be bought.

Once, in a hospital cafeteria that never closed, I sat across from an old woman who was waiting for her husband to come out of a procedure, and without any preamble she told me about their honeymoon in 1963, about a hotel with a broken piano and a landlady who sang, about how he had proposed to her in a rowboat that was slowly taking on water and neither of them had mentioned it because the conversation was more important than the boat. She had not planned to tell me this. I had not planned to hear it. But the hour made us into a confessional without a priest, and when her husband came out—fine, fine, the doctors were pleased—she gathered her coat and said, "You should write that down. Stories sink if you don't write them down." Then she was gone, and I have written it down, and now it is yours.

---

I don't want to romanticize the night. I have sat in enough of those waiting rooms to know that the night is also where the worst news keeps its office hours. The phone that rings at three a.m. is not calling to chat. The night is when the body's quiet failures announce themselves, when the mind's quiet cruelties hold their meetings, when the lonely discover the precise dimensions of their loneliness the way a man in a dark room discovers the furniture: by collision.

But I have also come to think that we need the night's honesty, that a life lived entirely in daylight hours becomes a life of performances, and that the performances calcify. We become our job titles, our group chats, our curated surfaces. The night comes along and strips that off, whether we like it or not, and what is underneath is often shabby and often frightened and, very occasionally, unexpectedly clean. The way a beach is clean after a storm. Not tidy. Clean.

My father recovered, if that is the word, and lived another four years, and in those four years he did finish the sentence, more or less, though it took a night in a different hospital and a different kind of waiting, and what he said was not what I had imagined and was both less and more than a revelation. He said he had been happy. He said he had not been happy in the ways he had planned to be happy, and that the plans had been wrong, and that he was telling me this not as a lesson—he was explicit about that, he did not want to be a lesson—but as a weather report. This is how it was. This is how it is. The nurse will come soon. Hold my hand if you want.

It was four in the morning. The corridor light was the color of old teeth. Somewhere a machine kept its patient count of a heartbeat. I held his hand. I did not say anything wise. Outside, the city was in its draft form, waiting to be rewritten by the dawn, and I understood that some things are only sayable in the hours nobody claims, and that the waiting is not a corridor between rooms but a room of its own, furnished with vending machines and bad coffee and the slow education of the heart, and that we pass through it more often than we admit, and that we would be lost without the people who know how to sit in it and keep the light on.

# The Fourth Watch

There is an hour that belongs to almost no one. It arrives without ceremony, somewhere between the last insomniac's final turn of the pillow and the first bird's tentative testing of its throat. The Romans called it the fourth watch — *quarta vigilia* — the last of the four divisions of the night, the one that ran from roughly three until dawn. It was the hour sailors dreaded and the hour of miracles. It is the hour, even now, when the world runs on a skeleton crew, when the body's furnace burns lowest, when worries inflate to the size of cathedrals and ideas arrive unaccompanied, without their usual baggage of doubt. Most of us sleep through it. This is an essay in defense of staying awake for it, at least once.

I want to begin with a historical grievance. We used to live in this hour. We didn't merely pass through it; we inhabited it, with our own customs, our own name for it, even our own peculiar physiology. The historian Roger Ekirch, sifting through diaries, court records, medical texts, and letters going back centuries, found something that modern sleep science had entirely forgotten: before the spread of artificial light, people in Europe and beyond did not sleep in one uninterrupted stretch. They slept in two. There was a "first sleep," which began an hour or two after dusk and lasted perhaps three or four hours. Then people woke. They rose from bed or lay quietly, and for an hour or more they entered a state so familiar it had a name — "the watch," Ekirch calls it, though English speakers also spoke of it as the "first waking." People prayed. They talked. They smoked by the embers. They interpreted the dream they'd just had, made love with a leisure that daytime schedules rarely permitted, or simply lay thinking in the dark with what one diarist described as unusual contentment. Then came the "second sleep," which ran until dawn.

This was not an eccentricity of a few rural households. The pattern shows up in sixteenth-century Italy and nineteenth-century Nigeria, in French farmhouses and English towns, in medical texts that treated the interval between sleeps as the best time to converse with a physician about one's dreams. And when the laboratory researcher Thomas Wehr later placed modern volunteers in conditions without electric light — fourteen hours of darkness a night, for weeks — they drifted, within a month, into the same biphasic pattern. First sleep, a quiet watch marked by a hormonal stillness the waking brain almost never knows, then second sleep. The architecture had been there all along, waiting for the lights to go out.

What switched it off, of course, was light itself. Gaslight arrived in the early nineteenth century and began the colonization of the night; electricity finished the job. The hour that had been a shared human territory became a corridor most people now pass through unconscious, sealed inside a single consolidated sleep, the watch folded away like a service no longer offered.

But the hour did not empty out. It only emptied of *us*, mostly. What remains is worth cataloguing.

Consider who is awake. In every town of any size, a hidden population clocks in while the rest of us go dark. The baker has been at work since two, and by four the ovens are breathing heat into a street that hasn't decided yet whether it exists. In the hospital, a nurse walks the corridor at a pace learned specifically for these hours — quick enough to seem purposeful, slow enough not to wake anyone — and the hospital at four a.m. is a different building from the hospital at noon: more honest, more hushed, more dependent on small kindnesses. A woman in the maternity wing is in the long middle of labor, because labor, like so much else, prefers the dark; spontaneous births cluster in the night and early morning, as if the body remembers something the calendar has forgotten. Out on the water, a fisherman is hauling nets by instruments and memory. In a studio downtown, a radio host is taking a request from a trucker somewhere on the interstate, and the two of them, who will never meet, are keeping each other company in the oldest way the species knows, which is by talking into the dark.

Then there are the unscheduled: the new mother, the original night-shift worker, holding a warm bundle in the blue light of a hallway; the teenager lying rigid with embarrassment at three a.m. over something said at dinner; the man who has decided, for the fourth night running, that the sensation in his chest is definitely serious this time; the monk in a hilltop monastery who has been standing in choir since two, singing psalms by candlelight, because someone has to keep the watch on behalf of everyone who cannot. For a thousand years the night offices were sung in the fourth watch on purpose. *A thousand years in your sight are like a watch in the night*, says the psalm — and the monks, in their particular genius, decided that if the hour was going to be strange anyway, it might as well be filled with song.

The body has its own opinions about this hour, and they are not gentle ones. Core temperature bottoms out around four or five a.m., the low point of the daily cycle, which is why the bed suddenly feels colder than it did at midnight even though the room hasn't changed. Melatonin is still high. Asthma is at its worst; the airways narrow in the small hours with such regularity that nocturnal worsening is a diagnostic marker. The cardiovascular system is drifting toward its own fragile morning, which is one reason strokes and heart attacks cluster toward dawn. And cortisol, the hormone of alertness and of stress, begins its slow pre-dawn climb — which is, among other things, why so many of us snap awake at three or four feeling simultaneously exhausted and unbearably keyed up, as if an alarm has gone off inside the blood.

This is also why the mind, at four a.m., is not to be fully trusted, and yet is more interesting than it is at noon. Sleep researchers have shown that even modest sleep loss makes the brain's threat-detection system — the amygdala — markedly more reactive, while the prefrontal cortex, the dampening and contextualizing machinery, is running on fumes. The result is a mind that generates catastrophes with industrial efficiency and lacks the usual equipment for talking itself down. The unpaid bill becomes a bankruptcy. The odd look someone gave you on Tuesday becomes evidence of a crumbling friendship. The small pain in the side becomes, by 3:40, a matter for the obituaries. Ingmar Bergman named a film for this hour — *Hour of the Wolf* — and had his character describe it as the hour between night and dawn when most people die, when sleep is deepest, when nightmares are most real, when the sleepless are haunted by their deepest anguish, and when, in the same cruel mercy, most babies are born. He understood the double bookkeeping of the fourth watch: it is the hour of greatest vulnerability and the hour of arrival, the hour the demons keep and the hour the midwives keep.

But there is a second ledger, and it would be dishonest not to mention it. The same unraveling of daytime rationality that turns worries into monsters also, sometimes, turns the world into a place of unusual perception. Problems that seemed insoluble at nine p.m. unknit themselves at four. Writers and scientists have long testified to the strange lucidity of the small hours — not the tiredness-blunted thinking of the afternoon slump, but something more liquid, less defended. The hypnagogic state, that borderland between waking and sleep, has produced more than its share of insights; there is a reason so many traditions treat the threshold of sleep as a place of vision. At four a.m., on the edge of it, the mind is a house with the doors open. Things wander in. Some of them are demons. Some of them are the ideas you have been too busy all day to hear knocking.

And it is not only the human mind that is abroad. The fourth watch is when the non-human world holds its own great assemblies. Every night, in every ocean on earth, the largest migration of living things on the planet takes place, and almost no one sees it. Copepods, lanternfish, small squid, krill — trillions upon trillions of creatures — rise from the safety of the deep midwater toward the surface to feed under cover of darkness, then sink again before dawn. By biomass, this nightly commute dwarfs the migrations of wildebeest and Arctic terns combined. Sonar operators in the mid-twentieth century kept detecting what they took to be a false seabed, a phantom floor a few hundred meters down that would not stay put; it was the deep scattering layer, the shadow of all that life in motion. The whole thing runs on the fourth watch. The sea, in other words, never accepted the invention of the electric light. It still keeps the old hours.

Closer to home, the city's fauna changes shift. The fox trots down the white line of an empty road with the confidence of a commuter. An owl delivers its single syllable into the silence and is answered from three gardens away. The cats, both the pampered and the feral, hold their parliament. Rats conduct their business along the same routes, night after night, with a conservatism that would impress a property developer. And somewhere in the middle of the fourth watch, the dawn chorus begins — not at dawn, but before it, in the dark, first one bird tuning up in the black like a musician checking strings before the hall fills, then a second, then the slow exponential bloom that will become, by first light, the loudest thing in the world. The dawn chorus is misnamed. It is a fourth-watch event. The birds start while the sky is still shut, as if they know something we have forgotten: that morning is not the beginning of the day but its announcement, and announcements are made in the dark.

It is worth sitting with how much of this we have lost, not because nostalgia is a program, but because the loss has a specific shape. A third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. The fourth watch used to belong to the stars the way noon belongs to the sun; it was the hour of astronomy and astrology, of navigation and mythology, of every culture's stories about what the night was for. When we lit the world, we didn't only push back the darkness. We pushed back a whole ecology of experience — the watch between sleeps, the sound of a town with no engines in it, the visible galaxy, the particular quality of thought that only exists when the rest of the village is unconscious. We traded it, and it was in many ways a fair trade: we got reading after dark, and safer streets, and hospitals that never close. But we should at least know what we sold.

Bergman's film takes its name from an old Scandinavian folk belief, and the folk had it right in more ways than the moderns: this is statistically an hour of dying, and an hour of birth, and an hour when the mind's ghosts walk. But the old belief also held that the hour of the wolf is when one is most alone — and the great modern invention, the thing we actually built in place of the watch, was the conviction that this hour is not for being awake in. Insomnia, in our culture, is not an experience. It is a defect. The person awake at four a.m. is a problem to be solved, a malfunction to be medicated, an anomaly to be corrected back into the consolidated eight hours that the light bulb made into a moral standard.

I am not romanticizing chronic insomnia, which is a genuine affliction and miserable in a way the well-slept rarely grasp. The specific loneliness of it — everyone you love asleep and unreachable, the house ticking and humming around you like a ship, the clock on the nightstand doing its slow arithmetic — is its own weather system. Clock-watching makes it worse; the fourth watch, measured in glances at a digital display, can last a geological age. If you suffer this way, much of what follows is not for you, or is for you only in the sense that you deserve better than the culture's contempt for the sleepless.

But for everyone else — for the person who is awake at four a.m. once in a season, uninvited, and lies there treating it as an emergency — there is another option, and it is the old one. Get up. That is what our ancestors did. They didn't lie in the dark cataloguing their failures; they rose, they put something on the fire, they did the quiet work of the watch. Make tea. Sit by a window. Write three sentences in a notebook, which at four a.m. will have a candor that daylight editing will later want to soften and which you should resist. Watch the sky over the rooftops and wait for the precise moment it stops being black and becomes something else — that first unnameable color, not gray, not blue, the color the fourth watch keeps as its secret. You will be joining a night shift that has been on duty since before there were cities: the bakers, the nurses, the monks, the fishermen, the mothers, the birds, the lanternfish rising in their billions toward a surface they believe is theirs. You will be, for one hour, a citizen of the country everyone else only sleeps through.

And then go back to bed, and sleep the second sleep, as they used to say, without guilt and without explanation. The watch was never meant to be a vigil of suffering. It was meant to be a room in the house of the night — a room most of us have forgotten is there, behind the door of three a.m., furnished with cold air and a different quality of silence and the sound of the first blackbird starting, somewhere, out of order, out of the dark, early.

# The Last Time You Do Anything, You Won't Know It

Somewhere, years ago, a father reached down and lifted his child onto his shoulders, and it was the last time he would ever do it. The child was four, maybe five — high enough now to see over the crowd, high enough to slap the leaves on the low branches. The father's hands closed around the small ankles. The child tugged his hair a little too hard, and he said *ow*, and the child laughed, and the day went on. Then the years went on. The child grew, as children do, in the ordinary way, which is to say invisibly, one unremarkable afternoon at a time, until one day the father reached down out of habit and the child was too big, or simply didn't reach back, and that was that. No one marked the occasion. There was no last ride, no photograph, no small ceremony in which the father said, *this is the last time I will carry you*, and the child said, *thank you for carrying me.* There was just a Tuesday. Then there were no more Tuesdays of that kind, ever again.

This is how nearly all of our last times happen: in disguise, on ordinary days, without announcement. You will do almost everything that matters in your life for the last time before you know you're doing it, and you will find out later — sometimes years later, sometimes never. The exits from the rooms of our lives are unmarked. There is no last call, no boarding announcement, no usher moving down the aisle with a flashlight to say this is the end of the show. Airports have last calls. Trains have last calls. Your life simply stops offering certain things and does not tell you.

Consider what else this is true of. Somewhere there was a last night someone read you a bedtime story. You were seven, maybe eight, maybe younger, and you had no idea that the era of being read to was closing over your head like water. Whoever was reading — a mother, a father, a grandmother with a voice like paper — closed the book, turned off the light, and went downstairs, and no one said, *well, that's the last of that.* There was a last time you genuinely needed someone to check under the bed for monsters, a last time the checking felt necessary rather than charming. There was a last time you were carried to bed asleep and woke up there without ever feeling the stairs. There was a last time someone cut the crusts off your sandwich without being asked. A last time you fit entirely on a hip. A last time a grown-up's hand was the thing you reached for at the edge of a curb, automatically, the way you reach for a rail in the dark. None of these were photographed. None of them were felt, at the time, as anything at all.

And then there is playing. Real playing — the whole-body, invented-world kind, the kind you cannot do on purpose as an adult. You had a friend once; everyone had this friend; and together you built a world and lived in it. Bikes in the driveway. A creek behind the houses. A fort of old boards. A video game, a card game, rules you invented and then defended like lawyers. And then one summer the family moved, or you moved, or school quietly scattered you into different hallways, and the last day of that world was a day like the others. You probably said *see you tomorrow.* You probably said *come over later.* The last day didn't know it was the last day. You might still remember the fort. You might remember one specific afternoon — the light through the boards, an argument about the rules, the exact sound of the creek — but you cannot isolate the last afternoon. It's in there with all the others, indistinguishable. Memory keeps the whole era but will not show you the door.

There was, for most of us, a stretch of years when all of our grandparents were alive. If you were lucky it was long. If you were very lucky you don't remember a time before it and you were grown before it ended. In that stretch there was almost certainly an afternoon — a holiday, a Sunday, a wedding, a funeral of somebody else — when all of them were in the same room with you at once. Someone was arguing about the thermostat or the gravy. The television was on. You were bored. You wanted to go play with the cousins, or get back to your book, or leave. And that room — that exact configuration of people breathing the same air, that specific arrangement of souls that had never existed before in the history of the universe — would never exist again. You were bored in it. This is not an accusation. You were a child, or you were busy, or you were twenty and immortal. It is only what the last times are usually like. They look like nothing. They feel like waiting.

Our whole culture is organized around firsts. First steps, first words, first day of school, first kiss, first job, first apartment. Firsts are anticipated, photographed, celebrated, put in albums and on refrigerators. We throw parties for them. Lasts get almost nothing. There is no party for the last time you do something. Retirements and graduations try to fill the gap, but they are staged lasts, lasts we scheduled, lasts we saw coming, which is a different species entirely. The real lasts — the ones that end eras rather than employment — never get a cake. Nobody stands up with a glass of wine and says, *to the last time we will all be in this house at once.* You don't find out you're finished with something until long after you're finished with it.

There is a last time you will sleep in the house you grew up in, and you will not know it. You will think you are visiting. You will think there will be other visits, other summers, other Christmases. And then there won't be — because the house is sold, or the people who made it a home are gone, or you simply stop, the way water stops running a certain way. Years later you will dream about that house, the way everyone does, and you will walk through it in the dream and touch the things, and the dream will be more vivid than any last visit you actually paid. Somewhere in you is the last night you slept there, and it was just a night. You had no idea you were saying goodbye to a building.

Later, there will be a last phone call with a person you love. It will be short. You will be in the car, or in the kitchen, doing something else with your hands. You will say the usual things, the maintenance things: I'm fine, work is busy, we should get together soon. And one of you will say *okay, love you, bye* — the way you say it, the way you've said it a hundred times — and hang up, and that will be the last time you hear that voice say your name, and you will not know. Weeks or years later, when the voice is gone, you will go looking for that call and find that it isn't there. Not really. It was too ordinary to keep. The mind files the extraordinary and discards the Tuesday. You will have the voicemails if you are lucky, if somebody thought to save them. Mostly you will have the fact of the call, the knowledge that it happened, and no recording of it in you. This is one of grief's particular cruelties: it sends you searching for the last time, and the last time was never saved.

Because that is part of what grief is. Not all of it, and maybe not the deepest part, but a real part: the search for the last time. We go back through the files. We ask each other, when did you last talk to him, what did she say, were you there, did you know, was I kind. We want the last time to have been a good one — to have been noticed, to have been worthy of what it was the last of. Sometimes it was. Often it wasn't. Often it was a rushed call in the car, a wave from a driveway, a *see you at Christmas* called across a parking lot. And then there is the work of forgiving ourselves for not knowing, for not being ceremonious, for being ordinary in the face of the end of an era. We weren't supposed to know. That is the design. Knowing this doesn't help, and we know that too, and we grieve anyway.

Here is the strange mercy in it. If we knew — if some quiet voice announced each last time as it happened — we could not bear it. *This is the last time your mother will carry you.* *This is the last night of the reading-aloud era.* *This is the last time all four of your grandparents will be alive in the world with you.* *This is the last time you will speak to your friend.* We would cling. We would ruin the moment trying to make it a monument. We would say the wrong enormous thing. The goodbye would be too heavy to lift. Life is livable in part because the last times come dressed as nothing, because we get to say *see you later* and mean it, because the ending is always officially somewhere else. The mind is kind this way. It lets us put one foot in front of the other. It files the endings where we don't have to look at them. Imagine being told, at every parting, *this is the last time.* You couldn't do it. You would never let go of anything. You would never get in the car. You would miss the last time trying to make the last time perfect.

You have heard the advice: live every day as if it were your last. It is good advice the way a fireworks show is a lighting plan. No one can do it. If you lived every day as your last you would quit your job within the week, say the unsayable things, eat dessert first, call people at two in the morning, sell the house, and in a month you would be broke, apologizing, and profoundly tired of dessert. The advice fails for a simpler reason, too. Real last days do not tell you they are last days. You cannot live a day as your last unless you know, and you never know.

We are, it turns out, creatures who can only value the ordinary once it has been certified as ending. Put a demolition notice on a building and suddenly everyone in the city is a photographer. Announce that a restaurant is closing and there will be a line down the block on the last weekend that the place never saw in ten years of being good. The notice changes the seeing. The last times that matter most, though, never get the notice. They do not have a last weekend. They happen on a Tuesday, to people who think they have all the time in the world, and they are gone before anyone thinks to take the picture.

There is a softer version of this, too. Every day you see people for the last time — the person in the next lane, the barista, the man who walks the same hour as you do by the river — and you will never know which strangers you have already seen for the last time. Somewhere behind you, in the crowd of faces you can't quite place, are people whose last appearance in your life has already happened. You shared a crosswalk with them. You waited for the same elevator. That was the whole relationship, and it's over, and it was nothing, and it was the only one of its kind.

What helps, then, is something smaller and stranger than the poster. Every so often, on an ordinary day, you catch it — not the fact that everything ends, which is too big and too vague to be of any use, but the possibility that *this specific thing* is happening for the last time in this form. The last swim of the summer, though you don't know it's the last. The last dinner at that table with those people. The last time the dog will jump onto the bed. The last time your child will say a word wrong — *pasghetti*, *aminal* — and you will correct it, gently, automatically, and the wrong word will be gone forever, replaced by the right one, and you will miss the wrong one more than you would have believed possible. You cannot live like this constantly. Constant reverence would flatten everything; if every moment is sacred, none is. But sometimes — maybe — you can treat an ordinary Tuesday as if it might be album-worthy. You can look up from the phone. You can answer the call. You can go to the thing. You can hold a moment with a slightly wetter eye than it strictly deserves. Simone Weil said that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. She might as well have been talking about this. Attention is the closest thing we have to a ceremony for the unmarked.

It is worth saying plainly: you are inside last times right now. This hour contains them. Something you did today — something small, something you would not list if someone asked what you did today — you will never do again in quite that way. A particular grouping of people. A particular light through a particular window. A particular version of yourself, which is already gone, which was gone by this evening. Yes, everything flows; yes, you cannot step in the same river twice; the Greeks covered that. But the abstract truth that everything changes is philosophy. The last time your grandmother will say your name is a fact with a date on it, and you will miss it. The last time your group of friends will all be in one city is a fact with a date on it. The last time the house will hold you the way it holds you now — that is a fact with a date on it. You will not see the date. You will live through it. You will call it nothing.

So: somewhere, tonight or some night soon, a father will lift a child onto his shoulders for the last time. Neither of them will know. The child will see the parade, or the lights, or the crowd, the world from up there one final time — the back of a head, the roar going by, a piece of confetti coming down — and then come back to earth and ask for ice cream and forget. The father's shoulders will ache a little, the way they always do now, and he will put the child down, and that will be the end of an era that took years and took no time at all. It is alright. It is not alright. Both of those are true, and they will both be true about almost everything that ever ends.

The least we can do — the only thing we can do — is be there for the ordinary while it still feels like nothing. Because that is the only place the last times ever happen. They never send an invitation. They never ask if you have a minute. They just arrive, dressed as a Tuesday, dressed as a call you almost didn't answer, dressed as a child on your shoulders asking you to walk toward the music.

And maybe, once in a while, when someone reaches down, you reach back. Not because you know. Because you don't, and you have decided to be someone who reaches back anyway.

# The Slow World

This morning I watched a snail cross a flagstone for what must have been forty minutes. It never hurried. It never paused to consider whether the journey was worth it, whether the other side of the stone offered anything better than the begonia leaf it had apparently abandoned, whether there was some more efficient route it had failed to consider. It moved the way a minute hand moves, which is to say it moved the way it was built to move, without any sense that movement could be otherwise. I almost missed it. I almost stepped on it. And then I almost walked past it, because a snail on a flagstone is the kind of thing the eye learns not to see, the way it learns not to see the grain of wood or the individual blades of a lawn or the particular shape of the clouds on an ordinary Tuesday.

But I stopped. And stopping, I entered a different country.

---

We tend to assume that the world happens at our speed. This is perhaps the most durable illusion we carry, more durable even than the illusion that the sun circles the earth, because at least that one got corrected. The assumption of shared tempo is subtler. We notice things that move as we move, things that appear and disappear on the scale of a conversation, a meal, a commute, a season. A bird crosses the yard. A flower opens. A friend's hair goes gray. These fit inside the human window, and so we treat them as the inventory of the visible world.

But the window is arbitrary. It is an accident of our neural architecture and our lifespan and the particular problem we evolved to solve, which was not "apprehend the full range of processes occurring in the universe" but rather "don't get eaten, find something to eat, and recognize the face of your grandmother." We are tuned, roughly, to the speed of things that might matter to a primate on a savanna. Everything outside that band is either a blur or a stone.

The stone, it turns out, is not a stone.

---

Consider the lichen. A lichen is not a plant. It is not even a single organism, depending on how you draw the boundaries of self. It is a fungus and an alga (or a cyanobacterium, or sometimes both, and sometimes a yeast thrown in for reasons no one fully understands) living together so intimately that they produce a body neither can produce alone, a body that has no name in ordinary speech except the name we give the partnership itself. The fungus provides structure, shelter, mineral acquisition. The alga provides sugar, manufactured from light and air. Together they colonize surfaces where nothing else will go: bare rock, the roof of the world, the walls of buildings we have abandoned, the shells of tortoises, the backs of certain beetles who have taken to farming them.

A lichen grows, in many species, at a rate measured in fractions of a millimeter per year. Some of the individuals on a given rock in the Arctic or the high Alps or the Atacama may be older than the pyramids, older than agriculture, older than the invention of the wheel. They have been there the whole time, doing what they do, at a pace that makes a redwood seem hasty. A human life is to such a lichen as a single afternoon is to us. Whole civilizations rise and fall in the time it takes a lichen to decide, in whatever sense lichens decide, to extend itself a millimeter further across the stone.

We walk past these beings. We sit down next to them on park benches and old stone walls. We lean against them at the summit of mountains we have spent days climbing, feeling accomplished, and they have not noticed our arrival in any sense that means anything to them. Our entire dramatic appearance and disappearance is too fast for them to register, the way a hummingbird's wing is too fast for us to see as anything other than a shimmer.

---

The trees are slower than us but faster than the lichens, and they have been having an entirely different experience of the same afternoon.

We now know, though we are still learning how to talk about it without sounding like we've been in the woods too long, that trees communicate. They release chemical signals through the air when they are attacked by insects, and neighboring trees, receiving those signals, begin producing defensive compounds before the insects arrive. They trade sugar and water and chemical messages through networks of fungi threaded through the soil — mycorrhizal networks, sometimes called, in the phrase that launched a thousand documentaries, the wood wide web. A dying tree will, in some forests, dump its stored carbon into the fungal network, a last transfer of wealth to its neighbors, including, remarkably, to trees of other species. A mother birch can recognize, it appears, her own seedlings, and send them more sugar than she sends to strangers.

None of this happens on our clock. A chemical conversation between trees may take hours, days, a whole growing season. When we walk through a forest and hear, as we say, nothing, we are like someone standing in a room where two people are speaking very slowly in a language we don't know, the words so drawn out that we take the silence between them for silence itself. The forest is not silent. The forest is speaking at the speed of trees.

There is a serviceberry in my neighborhood, or a serviceberry that was in my neighborhood, that came down in a storm two winters ago. The city ground it into mulch within a week. From our perspective the tree ended. From the perspective of the fungal network it fed and was fed by, from the perspective of the lichens on its bark (now drying on the woodpile, still technically alive in some fraction of their extent), from the perspective of the woodpecker cavities it housed, the ending is more like a change of address. Death itself is a matter of timescale. The atoms do not notice. They have appointments elsewhere, on schedules we cannot keep.

---

Geology is the study of things so slow that for most of human history we did not know they were things at all. Mountains were features, like the furniture of a room. It took an enormous act of imagination — the collective work of minds like Hutton and Playfair and Lyell and later the silent, stubborn Mary Anning — to see that the hills were falling down, that the valleys were being carved by water in real time, that the earth was not a finished stage but a process, an event still occurring.

Hutton, standing at Siccar Point on the Scottish coast in 1788, looked at angular unconformities — places where tilted layers of ancient seabed had been planed flat and then buried under newer rock — and understood, in what he called an abyss of time, that the world was unimaginably old. The realization was so large that it made people unwell. It is one thing to accept that the universe is 13.8 billion years old as a figure. It is another to stand in front of a cliff and feel the age of it in the body, to understand that the smooth stone under your hand was once mud at the bottom of an ocean that no longer exists, pressed and lifted and folded and eroded, and that the erosion you can watch happening in a rainstorm is the same erosion that carved the valley you live in, at the same pace, without hurry, without pause.

A glacier is a place where this becomes almost visible. Glaciers move fast enough that you can measure their motion year to year, slow enough that you can walk on them, and they are at the moment of this writing disappearing. The ice that took ten thousand years to accumulate is coming off in a human lifetime. We are, uniquely in the history of the planet as far as we know, a species that can watch geological time collapse. The slow world is being made to move at our speed, which is to say it is being destroyed. The lichens on the rocks that emerge from beneath a retreating ice sheet will take centuries to arrive, and the ice will not come back on any timescale that includes us.

---

At the other end of the spectrum, the world is too fast to see.

A hummingbird's wing completes a full stroke in something like a tenth of a second, fifty times a second in some species, and our visual system cannot parse it. We see a blur, a hum, a jewel that hovers by some apparent violation of physics. A honeybee's wing is faster still. A fly, when it takes off as your hand approaches, has already processed the threat, decided, and launched before your nervous system has finished reporting that the hand has begun to move. The fly, in a very real sense, experiences your sudden swipe as a slow and ponderous event, a lumbering giant in a slowing film. Its time is not your time.

Down at the scale of molecules, the speeds become almost comical. A typical enzyme can catalyze thousands of reactions per second. Light itself, crossing the width of a single cell, takes nanoseconds. The action potentials firing down your optic nerve as you read this sentence are traveling at speeds of up to 120 meters per second, and the fact that you experience reading as a smooth and continuous present is an achievement of the nervous system, a kind of rendering. The present moment, the "now" in which we live, is not a thin blade cutting between past and future. It is a construction, a buffer of several hundred milliseconds in which the brain binds together signals that arrived at different times so that they can be experienced as simultaneous. We are all living slightly in the past, and the past we live in has been edited for continuity.

There are creatures for whom our entire lives are a flicker. There is a species of deep-sea shrimp, and certain other crustaceans, whose temporal resolution is so fine that the flicker of a fluorescent light, which we perceive as steady, is to them a throbbing strobe. There is no telling what else we look like to them. Gods of tremendous slowness, perhaps, moving through their world like weather.

---

The human tempo, then, is not the middle of anything. It is not a standard. It is a habit of attention that happens to match the speed at which our bodies move through space and the speed at which our lives unfold toward their end. We built clocks that mirror us — the second roughly the pace of a heartbeat, the day the pace of our waking, the year the pace of our seasons — and then we treated those clocks as descriptions of reality rather than portraits of ourselves.

But attention can travel. This is, I think, one of the few genuine freedoms we have. The snail this morning pulled me, for forty minutes, out of human time. I watched the way its foot rippled, a wave of muscle traveling the length of its body, a process that under a lens would be beautiful and that at our distance is just "a snail moving." I watched the glisten it left behind, already drying at the far end of its trail. I noticed, for the first time in years of walking that path, the tiny fern growing in the crack of the flagstone, a fern that has been there, the gardener later told me, since before the stone was laid, coming up through a joint in the mortar. That fern is perhaps ten years old. The stone is perhaps a hundred. The limestone it was cut from is perhaps two hundred million. Three timescales, stacked like transparencies, and I had been walking over all of them as if they were one flat surface called "the path."

This is what I think the poets were always trying to say, in their various ways, about wildness and attention and the unexamined life. It is not that nature is morally instructive, or that snails have wisdom to offer, or that we should all go touch grass as a form of therapy, though none of that is wrong exactly. It is that the world is larger than the window, and that the window is not the world, and that the effort to see around the edges of our own tempo is an effort to become real. The lichen does not need us to notice it. The glacier does not grieve our inattention. But we need the noticing. We need it the way a person shut in a small room needs a window opened, not because the room will otherwise kill us but because the room is not all there is, and something in us knows it, and the knowing is a low hum of unease we learn to ignore.

---

The snail reached the far edge of the flagstone and dropped over the side, down into the dark soil and the hostas, going wherever snails go at noon. I do not know what it experienced, if anything it experienced, of the large primate who had crouched beside it for the better part of an hour. Probably nothing, or nothing we would recognize as an experience of being watched. To the snail, if there is something it is like to be a snail, I was weather. I was a warm stillness in the air, a shadow, a change in the light. Then I was gone, the way a cloud is gone, and the day went on without me in it, the day that had been going on without me in it for the whole time I was not crouching there, and that will go on without me in it for all the time I am not crouching anywhere, which is almost all of the time there is.

That is not a sad thought, or I am trying to make it not a sad thought. It is a thought about proportions, and proportions can be a kind of comfort. The lichen does not mind that we are brief. The mountain does not mind that we are soft and quick. The shrimp in the deep does not resent our blindness to its strobe-lit world. Everything is brief from some vantage and eternal from none and endless from the inside, and the inside is the only place we actually live.

I went inside eventually. I made coffee that had already gone lukewarm in the pot. The afternoon proceeded at the usual insulting speed, that steady fall of moments that we call ordinary time, and I tried, not very successfully, to remember the texture of the snail's foot, the ripple, the patience, the complete absence of the question that gnaws at everything we do, which is whether we will arrive in time. The snail does not live in time. The snail lives in the traveling. I would like to live more in the traveling. I will forget this by tomorrow. The fern in the wall will still be there. The lichen on the north side of the stone will have grown, if at all, by a width that could not be seen. The world will continue at all of its speeds at once, the fast, the slow, the geological, the molecular, the vast majority of it forever outside the window, going on without us, going on without needing us, going on.

# The Hours That Don't Count

There is a version of you that exists only between two and four in the morning. You have met this person. Everyone has. You wake for no reason, or for a reason you will never be told, and the ceiling above you is briefly a stranger's ceiling, and the thoughts that arrive are not the thoughts you would recognize as your own in daylight. They are faster, stranger, more credulous. A problem you couldn't solve at noon opens like a flower. A worry you didn't know you were carrying presents itself with itemized receipts. The house makes sounds it doesn't make at noon — the refrigerator's small cough, the water in the walls shifting its weight, a car passing with the particular loneliness of a car at 3 a.m., when a passing car means one car and not traffic.

I have spent a fair amount of time in those hours, not entirely by choice, and I have come to think of them as nobody's hours — hours that don't quite count, that the day refuses to acknowledge, that leave no official record. You can live an entire life and never once be asked what you did at 3 a.m. last night. The question would be almost indecent. And yet some of the most honest thinking I have ever done happened there, in the dark, to an audience of no one, and was gone by breakfast.

## The Other House

The house at night is a different house. This is not a metaphor. The floorboards speak a different language. The hallway is longer, or shorter; I have never decided which. Light behaves badly. You turn on the kitchen light and it seems too loud, not the sound of it but the fact of it, a yellow room floating in a black field, and you feel like a burglar in your own home, which in a sense you are — you have broken in on the house's real life, the life it lives when you are not watching.

Everything in the refrigerator looks more interesting at night. I don't know why this is. A pickle, at noon, is a pickle. A pickle at 3 a.m., eaten standing up, in the open door's cold light, with the rest of the house sleeping, is a small transgression, almost a ceremony. There is a whole genre of human experience that happens standing at an open refrigerator in the dark, and nobody writes it down.

When I was a child I used to wake in the night and walk through the house on a tour of inspection. I had a specific route: down the hall, past my parents' door (I would listen — not for anything in particular, just to hear the two-beat rhythm of two people breathing), through the living room where the furniture sat in the dark like animals pretending to be asleep, into the kitchen, where I would stand at the window and look at the backyard. The backyard at night was a foreign country. The swing set, which by day was just a swing set, an object of no mystery, became at night a structure of negative space, its shadows making a second swing set on the grass, and I understood, in the wordless way children understand things, that the world had a night version of itself that was older and less explained.

I never woke anyone. That was the rule I set for myself, though no one had set it for me. The point of the tour was to confirm that the house was still there, that it continued to exist without me, that the adults had not dissolved when the last light went out. Then I would go back to bed and sleep the way children sleep, which is to say completely, like a stone dropped into a well.

## The Great Forgetting

What strikes me now, looking back at that child, is not the nighttime walking but the completeness of the return. Every morning the night version of me was folded away like a letter, and the day version woke with no memory of the expedition, or only the faint sense of having been somewhere, the way you wake from a dream of a city you have never visited and can almost see.

We are built to forget the night. This is practical, of course. A species that carried its 3 a.m. thoughts into the marketplace would not get much done. The daylight mind is a press secretary, smooth and sensible, and it does not appreciate what the night mind says. So we perform, every morning, a small and total amnesty. The anxieties that seemed like revelations are demoted to "something I was worrying about." The ideas that seemed like genius are discovered, in the light, to be either obvious or insane, and usually both.

But I think something is lost in the amnesty, something more than bad ideas. The night mind is not just a distorted version of the day mind. It is a different instrument. It has no audience, and therefore no self-consciousness, or a different one. It is not trying to be consistent. It is not managing a reputation. It can hold two contradictory beliefs at once, not because it is confused but because it has not yet been asked to choose. Psychologists talk about the "default mode network," the brain's screensaver, the network that lights up when we are not focused on a task. At night, in the dark, in the half-waking state, this network runs unsupervised. It is the closest we come, while still being ourselves, to being someone else.

The writer who understood this best may have been Kafka, who did his writing at night and who described his nighttime work as a kind of authorship *of* himself rather than by himself — the sentences arriving as if dictated. And there is a long tradition, from Coleridge to the present, of the night offering a draftsman's access to material the daylight self would have refused at the door. "Kubla Khan" came to Coleridge in an opium dream; he sat down to write it out and was interrupted by "a person on business from Porlock," and the poem remains a fragment. I have always suspected the person from Porlock was the daylight self, arriving to collect him.

## First Sleep, Second Sleep

It was not always this way. The historian Roger Ekirch, sifting through centuries of court records, diaries, and letters, found something that had been hiding in plain sight: before the modern era, in Europe and likely elsewhere, people did not sleep in one block. They slept in two. There was a "first sleep," which began a couple of hours after dusk, and then, around midnight, people woke for a while — an hour, two — and then returned to a "second sleep" until dawn.

The waking interval was not considered insomnia. It was considered the night. People got up. They prayed, they read, they talked, they visited neighbors, they made love, they smoked, they lay thinking. There are old prayers specifically for the "watch" between sleeps. Farmers believed this was the best time to plan the next day's work, and there is some modern evidence they were right — the interval is rich in calm, meditative thought, the hormone melatonin still high, the mind in a state that one researcher compared to something like meditation.

Then came the streetlamp, and the factory whistle, and finally the electric light, and the two sleeps were pressed into one. We did not just light the night; we abolished it, or abolished our old relationship with it. The hour of waking between sleeps did not disappear. It went underground. It became the 3 a.m. wake-up, the one we now treat as a malfunction, a symptom, a thing to be cured with a pill or a white-noise machine or the blue-light discipline of a sleep hygienist. We have medicalized what used to be simply the middle of the night, the watch, the time when the house's real life went on.

I find this both consoling and a little sad. Consoling, because my 3 a.m. wakefulness has ancestors; it is not a defect in me but an atavism, a room in the old house of sleep that the modern floor plan no longer includes. Sad, because the room is still there, and we no longer know what it is for. We wake into it and lie in the dark checking our phones, feeding the daylight self a little light so it will go back to sleep, when the hour was once the hour of lamps and prayers and quiet conversation, the hour of the second life.

## The Republic of the Sleepless

There is a republic you never hear much about, because its citizens are scattered and mostly silent: the people for whom night is a workplace. The nurse doing her third twelve-hour shift of the week. The baker who starts at 2 a.m. so the bread will exist by 7. The trucker running a dark interstate, talking on the radio to other trucks, other dark cabs. The printer, the stocker, the security guard, the 911 dispatcher, the newspaper editor of a shrinking paper, the gas station attendant, the woman at the hospital desk who slides a form across the counter to a man who has just learned something terrible and is trying to understand his insurance.

I spent one long night in a hospital waiting room once, and I have never forgotten the physics of that room. It was the middle of the night and the waiting room was full, which told me everything I needed to know about the world: that at any given moment, in every city, there is a room like this, full of people in the strange suspension of not-yet-knowing, and that the day, when it comes, will split them into the relieved and the shattered, but that for now they are all equal, all in the same amphibious state between the life they had at dinner and the life they will have at breakfast. A vending machine hummed. A television played with the sound off. A man in work boots slept sitting up, his chin on his chest, and a woman next to him — I never learned if they were strangers or spouses — occasionally reached over and, without looking, adjusted the newspaper on his lap so it would not slide to the floor.

The republic of the sleepless has its own etiquette. Voices are lower. Kindness is more direct, because there is no time to be polite and no one to perform for. The nurse who comes out to call a name does not use the bright daytime voice; she uses the night voice, which is quieter and somehow more honest. And when dawn comes, and the waiting room fills with the day shift, and the fluorescent lights seem suddenly too many, the night people go home to their darkened bedrooms and the day people take over, and the two populations barely overlap. They pass each other in the parking lot. They know almost nothing of each other's worlds.

We structure our whole civilization around the assumption of a shared schedule, and then we staff the edges of it with people who live on the broken hours, and we call them night owls or shift workers or insomniacs, as if the difference were a personality trait and not a whole alternative citizenship.

## What the Night Knows

I do not want to romanticize this. A great deal of what the night mind produces is garbage. The 3 a.m. brain is a credulous brain; it will believe the worst, it will rehearse conversations that will never happen, it will find in a mild comment made at dinner a document of betrayal. Anyone who has lain awake dismantling a relationship, a friendship, a career, over a single unanswered text message, knows the night mind's talent for prosecution. It is a brilliant lawyer and a terrible judge.

But even the prosecution has its uses. The things we worry about at night are not random. They are the day's unsorted mail. The daylight self is a genius at deferral — it can take a grief, a jealousy, a decision not yet made, and place it in a drawer, and the drawer closes with a click that sounds a lot like peace. The night opens the drawers. Not all of them, but the ones that matter, the ones that have been shut too long. This is unpleasant. It is also, I think, necessary. A person who never meets their 3 a.m. mind is a person who has a great deal of unexamined mail.

There is a particular kind of clarity that only happens at night, and it is not the clarity of analysis. It is the clarity of reduced circumstances. So much of what we think during the day is social thinking — what so-and-so thinks of us, what we will say in the meeting, how the sentence will land. Strip all that away, take away the audience, take away even the anticipation of an audience, and what is left is smaller and stranger and more true. At night you can admit things. The admission does not fix them. But the day self, the press secretary, cannot fix what it has not been told.

I once read that some monasteries keep a practice of rising in the dark for the night office, the vigil, and that the monks say the darkness is part of the prayer — that certain things can only be said, or understood, without light. I am not a monk. But I have had the experience, in the hour before dawn, of a sentence forming that I knew I would not be able to say in daylight, not because it was forbidden but because the daylight self would not find it credible. It would sound like poetry, or like whining, or like something read in a book. At 4 a.m. it was simply true.

## Dawn, the Great Reabsorption

And then the light comes, and it all goes under.

There is a specific minute — I have caught it perhaps a dozen times, usually by accident, staying up rather than getting up — when the night ends not with a decision but with a dissolve. The window, which has been a black mirror all night, your own face faintly ghosted on the glass, begins to admit the world again. First the sky is not-black, then it is gray, then it is a color, and the room, which had been an idea of a room, becomes a room. The furniture resumes its daylight identity. The swing set is just a swing set. And the night mind, the other you, does not exactly leave. It goes down. It goes wherever it goes during the day — the basement of the self, the place the drawers are — and the press secretary clears his throat and the day begins.

I have tried, from time to time, to smuggle something across that border. I have kept a notebook by the bed, as the writing guides instruct, and written in the dark, and in the morning found pages of pencil marks, urgent-looking, sometimes a whole sentence, once a word repeated twenty times. The sentences that survive are rarely the ones that seemed important. The one I remember best said only: *the house is not the house.* Which I take to mean something, still, though I could not tell you what the night self intended, and the day self has decided it is a fine title for something and has done nothing with it.

Maybe that is the right relationship. We are not meant to be night people and day people at once, fully. We are meant to be day people who receive occasional, unreliable dispatches from the night, and who act on them imperfectly, the way you act on a dream. The monk rises in the dark and carries the vigil into the day's work. The nurse finishes her shift and sleeps through the brightest hours and wakes at dusk with the whole day already spent, a citizen of the other republic, and learns, over years, the particular freedom of walking to the store at 10 p.m. under a sky nobody is using.

## An Inventory of Small Hours

If I were to make an inventory of what the hours that don't count have given me, it would look like this:

The knowledge that my house has a night version, and that I am a guest in it.

The memory of my father, or rather the sound of my father, coming down the stairs once at 3 a.m. when I was grown and visiting, and finding me awake at the kitchen table, and not asking why, only putting the kettle on, so that we drank tea in the dark without turning on the light, and spoke in the low register that only exists between people who are awake when they should be asleep, and said nothing of importance, and it remains one of the more complete conversations of my life.

The understanding that worry is often just thinking that has lost its manners, and that some of it, seated and given tea, will admit it only wanted attention.

The glimpse, in a hospital waiting room, of the human race in its nightclothes, unimpressive and unguarded and carrying each other's coats.

The suspicion, which I cannot prove, that everyone I meet is carrying around a whole nighttime country they will never show me — a country of rehearsed speeches and old songs and replayed arguments and sudden mercies — and that when they are tired or ill or old, the border gets porous, and the country leaks out in odd comments and unexplained tears and laughter at nothing, and that this is not senility or weakness but the other self coming up for air.

And the certain knowledge, which the daylight self will call a cliché and the night self will call a fact, that a person is not one thing. That the you reading this and the you who will wake at 3 a.m. are not the same, and that the second one is not a malfunction of the first. That the second one has things to say, most of them difficult, a few of them true, and that the whole art of being a person may be nothing more than learning to take the night self seriously without letting it drive, and to take the day self seriously without letting it forget the house has a basement, and the basement has a window, and once in a while, in the smallest hours, there is a light on down there, and someone is home.
