# The Four O'Clock Republic

There is an hour that belongs to almost no one. Four a.m. sits in the gap between the late night and the early morning, too late for the faithful and too early for the industrious. The bars have closed. The bakeries have not yet opened their doors, though their ovens are already thinking about bread. Some languages call it the hour of the dog — the hour when even the night's watchers grow quiet.

If you are awake at four, you are awake for a reason, and the reasons are rarely small.

In a hospital on the east side of the city, a nurse walks the corridor with a paper cup of water in one hand and a small white pill in the other. The lights have been dimmed to their nighttime amber. She knows the sounds of this hour: the hum of the machines, the squeak of one specific wheel on one specific gurney she has asked maintenance to fix three times, the breathing of strangers. At 4:12 she wakes a man to give him his medication, and he looks at her with the naked confusion of the deeply asleep, and she waits while he returns from wherever he was, and she says, *You're in the hospital, you're okay, it's just your pills.* She has said this eleven thousand times. She will say it again tomorrow. There is a version of tenderness that looks, from the outside, exactly like routine.

Twelve blocks away, a woman sits upright in a dark living room with a baby against her shoulder. The baby is six weeks old and has decided, provisionally, that night is for crying. The woman has stopped keeping track of days. She knows only two times now: the baby is asleep, and the baby is awake. The city outside the window is a gray nothing. She hums something without a melody — an old commercial jingle from her childhood, degraded by decades into something almost like a lullaby. She is more tired than she has ever been, and she is also, in a way she will not be able to explain later, completely awake, more awake than she has been since she was a child lying in bed the night before her birthday. Love at four a.m. is not sentimental. It is biochemical, muscular, a matter of standing when standing is the last thing the body wants. She stands. She walks the perimeter of the room. The baby hushes, briefly, then doesn't.

On the highway outside the city, a truck driver drinks coffee from a cup that has been refilled so many times the paper has gone soft at the seam. The road is empty in a way roads never are during the day — empty like a stage between performances. He has been driving since ten. He will drive until six. At four a.m. the lines on the road become hypnotic, and he has tricks for this: he names the makes of the cars in the opposite lane, he recites the stops on the bus route he rode as a boy, he eats sunflower seeds one at a time and counts them. He is carrying frozen peas. He thinks sometimes about who will eat them — the thousands of households, the children who will push them around their plates. It is the closest thing he has to a family in this cab: this imagined table of strangers eating his peas.

In a house on a street lined with lindens, an old man sits at his kitchen table with the light off. He is not crying. He has done his crying in the daytime, in pieces, in the checkout line and the hardware store, which he has found is worse — the public crying, the embarrassed faces of cashiers. At four a.m. his wife has been dead for five months and eleven days, and the house makes its house sounds, and he sits in the dark because the dark is more honest. When the light is on he sees the two chairs. When the light is off there is only the window, and the window is a mirror, and the mirror only holds him. At 4:40 he gets up, because getting up is the work now, and makes tea he will forget to drink, and the kettle's whistle is the first clear note of the day.

At the airport, Terminal C is a cave of plastic chairs. A young man sits with a boarding pass for a flight that leaves at 6:15. He is moving to a city where he knows one person, a cousin of a friend, who has offered a couch for two weeks. He is twenty-three. His whole life is in a duffel bag that is too small for a whole life, which is why he chose it. He has not told his mother he is leaving today. He told her next week, to buy himself a day without the goodbyes, and now he is paying for that mercy in this plastic chair, composing and deleting a text message. A cleaning woman pushes her cart past him, slows, and looks at him with an expression he will not understand for another ten years — when he is the one pushing a cart, and a kid with a duffel bag is sitting alone at 4 a.m., and he slows down, and doesn't quite know why.

In the bakery on Ninth Street, the first batch is coming out. The baker has been awake since three, which she considers sleeping in; her father rose at two. She pulls the sheet pans and the smell goes down the empty street like a rumor, finding the grate of the coffee shop next door, the open window of the insomniac on the third floor, who will later swear he can still taste bread he never ate. The baker does not think of herself as feeding anyone in particular. She thinks in loaves. But somewhere in the city a man will bite into this crust at seven and feel, without knowing why, that the day is possible.

A fox crosses the boulevard at 4:31, pausing in the exact center of four empty lanes, and for a moment the whole republic has a mascot. The birds have not started. The birds start later, and they start all at once, as if taking a signal.

None of these people know about one another. That is the rule of the hour. They are a congregation that never assembles, a city within the city, sworn to no oath, flying no flag. They pass each other in the daylight and see only strangers, because they are strangers, because the four o'clock republic dissolves at dawn the way salt dissolves in warm water — completely, and without a trace, and into everything.

By five the sky has begun to compromise. By six the day people arrive, rubbing their eyes, and inherit a world that the night people kept for them: the hospital still running, the bread already cooling, the baby fed, the truck delivered, the dead man's widow still standing. Nobody thanks anyone. Nobody knows to.

But the hour will come again tomorrow. It always does. And the door of that hidden country will open again, without ceremony, for whoever cannot sleep, and whoever must rise, and whoever is simply standing at a window at four in the morning, holding a child, or a pill, or nothing at all, watching the last of the dark do its quiet work.

**The Night Desk**

The station sits at the edge of town, past the grain elevator, in a building that used to be a seed store. There is a 100-watt AM transmitter on the roof and a neon OPEN sign in the window that nobody ever sees, because nobody comes here at two in the morning except me.

I host the night shift. Have for eleven years. The show is called *The Night Desk*, which was the previous host's name for it, and I never changed it because I couldn't think of anything better and because the desk itself is a good desk — oak, scarred, older than the station, older probably than the town. Somebody carved a small, imperfect star into its corner sometime before I was born, and I touch it sometimes the way you'd touch a doorknob in the dark, just to confirm the world is still where you left it.

The format is simple. I play songs people request, and I take calls, and mostly I listen. You would be amazed what people will say to a voice on the radio at three in the morning. Things they can't say at the dinner table. Things they can't say in the daylight, when the face you're talking to is looking back at you and waiting to decide what it thinks.

There are regulars. There's a man named Dewey who drives a snowplow in winter and a gravel truck in summer and who calls most nights around two-thirty from whatever cab he's in, wanting Hank Williams. There's a woman, Roberta, who works the desk at the Motel 6 out by the interstate and who has seen, over twenty years, every variety of human arriving and leaving, and who tells me about them in a low, amused voice, never using names, never cruel. There's a teenager who calls from the closet of his family's house, phone pressed to his ear, and who never says much, but who stays on the line, and I have learned not to ask him why the closet, and I have learned to leave long spaces where he can talk if he wants to, and sometimes he does.

Tonight the sky is doing that thing it does in late October, where the stars seem closer and colder, arranged with a kind of indifference that is almost personal. The heater in the station clicks and hums. The coffee in my thermos has gone to that stage where it is no longer coffee but a kind of statement about coffee, bitter and formal. Dewey has already called. Roberta has already called. The teenager has already come and gone, four minutes of near-silence, and then the particular click of a phone being hung up gently, which is different from the click of a phone being hung up hard, and which I have come to prefer.

At 3:40 the phone rings again.

"We have a caller," I say, because that's what I say, and I punch the button. "You're on the Night Desk."

There's a pause. Then an old woman's voice, thin and clear, the way voices are on the radio at this hour, as if the person is not far away at all but standing just behind you in the room.

"Is this the girl who takes the requests?"

"It is."

"My husband used to listen to you. Before." She doesn't say before what. She doesn't have to. "He'd sit in the kitchen with the radio on and that little blue light, and he'd write things down. Numbers. He was a bookkeeper. Fifty-one years a bookkeeper, and then he retired and he still wrote things down, columns of them, for no reason, just to have the numbers go somewhere." Another pause. "He died in March."

"I'm sorry," I say. And I am. It is a strange grief, the grief for someone you never met but whose habits you know.

"He wanted me to tell you something, if I ever got up the nerve. He said you'd understand. He said, she sits in that building all night with the light on, she'll understand."

The heater clicks off. The transmitter hums on the roof. Somewhere out in the dark, I know, there are pickups on county roads, and a woman at the Motel 6 folding towels, and a boy in a closet with his knees drawn up, all of them with this same voice in their ears, this same old woman, and none of them knowing it.

"He said to tell you the light matters. The one you keep on. He could see it from the kitchen window, across the field. He said a town ought to have one light on somewhere all night, in case anybody's up. In case anybody needs to know somebody's up."

I look at the red bulb above the transmitter, the one the engineers call the pilot light. It's been burning since before I took this job. It will burn after I'm gone. I have never once thought of it as being for anyone.

"Tell him — " I start, and then I stop, because he can't hear me, and she knows it, and I know it, and the sentence has nowhere to go. So I say: "I'll keep it on."

"I thought you'd say that," she says, and there is something in her voice that might be a smile. "Play something by Patsy Cline. He liked her, though he'd never admit it. He'd write her name in the columns sometimes, instead of numbers, and then he'd act like he hadn't."

I find the song. "She's Got You." I cue it up and I talk over the intro, quiet, the way you talk when you think someone might be drifting off.

"That was Edna, calling in from east of the elevator, asking for Patsy Cline, for a bookkeeper who kept the numbers and the names in the same column, which is the right way to do it, if you ask me. This one's for him. And this one's for everybody up. You're not the only one."

I let the song play. I touch the little star on the corner of the desk. Outside, the field is dark all the way to the trees, and then beyond the trees it is dark all the way to the next town, and beyond that, more dark, more fields, more radios, more people awake in the long middle of the night, and one red light burning on a roof at the edge of town, for no reason, for every reason, in case anybody's up.

The coffee has gone cold. I drink it anyway. Four hours yet. The phone is quiet. The night is long, and someone is always up.

# Call Me Back

The message arrives on a Tuesday, which is the most insulting part. If grief had any manners it would come on a Sunday evening, at the end of a long weekend, when you are already lowered and the week has not yet gathered its arguments against you. Instead: Tuesday, 2:47 p.m., in the parking lot of the pharmacy, between a reminder about a dental cleaning and a coupon for the falafel place that closed last year.

The voicemail icon. One. I stand there with the bags pooling against my wrist and press play.

"I keep locking myself out of the car," my sister says. "I don't know what's wrong with me. Call me back. I want to tell you about the dream."

That's all. Eleven seconds. Her voice has the brightness it took on when she thought she was being ridiculous, which was her way of being brave about it. Then the click, the hum, the phone asking whether I want to save, delete, or share.

The timestamp says the message was left fourteen months ago. It sat somewhere — a tower, a cache, some drawer of the network where the world keeps what it isn't ready to give — and fell out today, the way the last of a season's snow comes off a roof in April, long after anyone is waiting for it.

My sister died fourteen months ago, in March. This message was left nine days before that.

I do the math four times in the parking lot, as if the numbers might reorganize themselves out of kindness. Nine days before. She was locking herself out of the car and dreaming something she wanted to tell me, and the network held it, and held it, and let it go on an ordinary Tuesday while I was buying sunscreen and a birthday card for a friend.

I almost call the number back. My thumb knows the way; it starts the motion out of the old muscle. Then I remember what the number is now — a line into silence, or worse, a line into someone else's pocket, some stranger who was assigned those digits when the company recycled them, the way the company does, the way the world does.

I don't call. I save the message. I drive home with the windows down even though it's cold, because my sister drove that way and it seemed like a thing to do with my hands.

For a week I play it more than I should. In the morning, before I get up. At night, when the house does its settling and I do mine. The dog has started lifting his head at the sound of her voice, then lowering it again, disappointed in a way he can't name and I can. Once I play it in the grocery store and have to stand a long time in front of the oranges.

People tell you the dead keep living in your phone. Nobody means it literally. Her number is still in my contacts. Her texts still sit in the thread, the last one a photo of a dog she met on the street, captioned *this guy*. If I hold the phone to my ear too long I start to hear things in the white noise — the octave of her, the shape of her sentences.

The lockouts were famous. She locked herself out of cars, houses, hotel rooms, once a boat. My father used to say she could get locked out of a tent. She'd call me every time, standing on a curb somewhere, laughing that laugh that was half fury, and I'd drive over with the spare key, and we'd get food, and it would become an evening. A whole architecture of evenings was built on her losing things. I did not know that was what the spare key was for. I thought it was for emergencies.

I never heard about the dream. There was no one left to hear about the dream.

On the fourteenth day I call the number. It's 3:12 a.m., which is not a decision so much as a failure to stay asleep. It rings. It rings with the patience of a line that has no idea what it is. Then a voicemail, a man's voice, unfamiliar, slightly hoarse, the recording of someone who does not know he has inherited the dead: *Hey, you've reached me. Leave it.*

The beep.

I hang up. I sit in the dark with the phone on my chest and think about what "leave it" means.

In the morning I call again, in daylight, like a person.

He answers on the second ring. I say, "I think you have my sister's old number," and he is quiet, and then he says, "I was wondering when someone would call for her."

He has had the number for a year. In that year he has received, he tells me, a dentist reminder, a delivery of flowers he sent back, a text from a book club asking if she finished the novel (she did not), and now me. He is not unkind. He is a man in a kitchen somewhere, holding a phone that keeps receiving the residue of a woman he never met. He says he sometimes wonders if he should record a different greeting, something easier for people like me.

People like me.

I ask him if I can leave a message. He says, "It's your sister's number," which is not an answer, and is one.

"I got your message," I say, after the beep. "Sorry it took so long to call back. I was —" and here the language fails, because there is no tense for this, no grammar for the place she is. "Call me when you can," I say. "I still want to hear about the dream."

I hang up. Outside, a Tuesday is ending, or a Wednesday is starting; the streetlight comes on the way it does, indifferent and orange and faithful.

Somewhere in the network, I have to believe messages are still moving. That they find their way back to the people they were meant for, the way water finds a low place, without any help from us.

Eleven seconds. I saved it. I will save it. Some things you don't get to keep and keep anyway.

**What the Crows Brought**

After Marta died, Ivo began leaving scraps on the back fence. Bread crusts, bacon fat, the heels of the cheese he could no longer finish. He did it without ceremony, the way you water a plant you aren't sure will make it. He told no one. His daughter called on Sundays and asked how he was managing, and he said *fine, fine, the garden keeps me busy*, which was true in the way most comforts are true—technically, and not at all.

The crows noticed first. Of course they did. They noticed everything.

They came in the low blue hour before sunrise, three of them at first, then seven, then a loose parliament of eleven. They did not sing. They did not thank him. They watched him from the persimmon tree with one eye and then the other, tilting their heads as though the world were a problem they were politely declining to solve. When he set the food down and went back inside, they dropped from the branches like black punctuation.

He began to look forward to it. This embarrassed him. Seventy-one years old, a retired land surveyor, a man who had spent forty years measuring the earth for other people's purposes, and now his mornings had narrowed to this: a fence, a handful of scraps, the cold, the birds, the fact of being needed in the smallest possible way.

In March, he found a button on the fence post. Brass, four holes, a thread of red still caught in one of them. He turned it in his palm. Crows, he knew, sometimes brought gifts to the people who fed them. He'd read a article once, or dreamed he'd read it. He put the button in the dish on the windowsill where Marta used to keep her thimbles, and thought nothing more about it—except that he thought about it constantly.

A week later, a shard of sea glass, blue as a gas flame. Then a bent coin from a country that no longer existed. Then a key.

The key stopped him. It was small, brass, the teeth worn almost smooth, and it was the size and shape of the key to the garden shed, which had been lost for nine years, which Marta had lost, which she had looked for in the last lucid week of her life with an urgency he had mistaken for confusion. *I need to lock up the tools, Ivo. Someone has to lock up the tools.* He had told her the door didn't lock anymore, that it didn't matter, that she should rest. She had looked at him with an expression he would spend the rest of his life unpacking.

He tried the key in the shed. It turned. The lock, which he had sworn was broken, opened as if it had only been waiting.

He did not tell his daughter. Some things you keep in the pocket of the day, unexamined, warm from your hand.

The gifts continued. A pearl earring, solitary. A fragment of pottery, glazed the green of deep water. A whisker, silver, coiled like a question. He lined them up on the windowsill in the order they arrived, a sentence in a language he couldn't speak but was slowly learning to read. The crows watched him from the tree as he arranged them, and he had the growing, unscientific certainty that they knew exactly what they were doing.

In April, his granddaughter came to stay for a week. She was nineteen, fracture-boned with grief she hadn't been offered a role in, and she spent the first two days on her phone in the room that used to be hers. On the third morning she appeared in the kitchen at dawn, drawn by the noise, and watched him carry the plate to the fence.

"You're feeding the crows," she said.

"I'm feeding the crows."

"Grandma hated the crows."

"Grandma hated the crows," he agreed. "She said they were spies."

They stood together in the cold and watched the birds descend. His granddaughter laughed, once, a short surprised sound, as the largest crow—a male, ragged at the shoulder, clearly in charge—hopped sideways down the fence toward them and fixed her with a look of ancient administrative displeasure.

"His name is Capo," Ivo said. He hadn't named the bird. The name had simply been waiting, the way names do.

By the end of the week she was up with him every morning. She started a notebook. *Gift log,* she wrote on the first page, and drew a small crow in the corner, and beneath it she catalogued each offering with the seriousness of a customs officer. He listened to her narrate the birds to herself—*that one's Biscuit, she always waits, that one flies crooked*—and he understood that she was learning something she could not have been taught on her phone, in her city, in the ordinary traffic of her life: that attention is a form of love, and that love does not require a reply.

On her last night, the crows left something new. She found it in the morning, on the fence post, exactly where the button had been: a wedding ring. Too big for a crow to have found by accident in a world full of dropped things, too old, too specific. Inside the band, worn almost to nothing, an engraving. He needed his reading glasses and a lantern and his granddaughter's steadier hands.

*M, con tutto il mio cuore.*

Marta. Marta, with all my heart. The ring he had put on her finger in a courtyard in Trieste in a rain that came down like applause. The ring she had stopped wearing in the last year because her fingers thinned and it slipped, and he had put it in the drawer of the bedside table for safekeeping, and then she was gone, and then the house was quiet in a way houses only get quiet once.

But the ring had been in the drawer. He was almost sure. He was almost sure he had seen it there, months ago, a dull gleam among the rubber bands and the spare batteries and the receipts she had kept for reasons no one could reconstruct.

Almost sure. And then not sure at all. And then not caring, in a way that felt like a door opening onto weather.

He put the ring on a chain and wore it under his shirt. His granddaughter photographed the windowsill, the fence, the persimmon tree, Capo sitting in it like a small angry god. She promised to come in the summer. She promised to tell her mother about the crows, and he said, *tell her, tell her everything,* and found that he meant it.

The birds came the next morning, as they always did. They ate. They watched. They waited for him to understand that the world keeps its own inventory, that nothing given is ever really gone, that even the smallest kindness is entered into a ledger kept by creatures who have been watching us since before we had words for watching.

He raised his empty hands to them, an old man's clumsy salute, and went in to put the kettle on.

**How to Whistle**

My grandfather taught me to whistle the summer I turned nine, on the porch of the house he would die in four years later, though neither of us knew that yet, or maybe he did and I didn't, which is a kind of knowing too.

"You have to make a tiny hole," he said. "Like you're keeping a secret, but only a small one. Not a big secret. A secret about a ladybug."

I made a hole. I blew. Nothing.

"You're blowing too hard. You're not trying to put out a fire. You're trying to call one to you."

I blew softer. My lips buzzed. A sound came out like a bicycle tire losing air.

He laughed, not unkindly. "Closer."

We sat there in the heat. The porch boards were the color of driftwood, soft with age, and if you pressed your thumb into one in the right place near the railing, the wood gave a little, like it had a pulse. My grandmother had died in March. Nobody said the word *died*. They said she passed, they said we lost her, they said it was a blessing, which is a word adults use when they want to bundle up a hard thing and put it on a high shelf.

The whistling was my idea. I had heard him do it in the garden the week before, a low looping tune I didn't recognize, and something in my chest had pulled tight, the way a curtain moves when a door opens in another room. I asked him to teach me. He looked at me for a long moment, and then he said, all right.

"Think of it like this," he said. "The breath doesn't go out. It goes over. Like a bird over a roof. The roof is your tongue."

I curled my tongue. I blew. The bicycle tire again, then a hiss, then — for one second — a note. Thin and wobbling, like a new thing testing whether it was allowed to exist.

"I did it!"

"You did it," he said, and there was something in his voice I couldn't name then. It wasn't pride exactly. It was more like relief. As if I had picked up something he'd put down a long time ago.

We practiced. He whistled the looping tune and I tried to follow. He told me he'd learned it from his mother, who learned it from a man on a ship coming over from somewhere I'd never heard of, and that the man on the ship had learned it from his brother, who was standing next to him, and that they whistled it back and forth across the deck at night to make sure the other was still there.

"That's a good reason to whistle," he said. "To make sure someone's still there."

I asked if Grandma could whistle.

He was quiet for a while. A car went by. The neighbor's dog said one word and then thought better of it.

"She could," he said finally. "She didn't much. She said it was a waste of a good breath. But the first time I took her out, she whistled at the moon. Just once. And I knew."

"Knew what?"

"That I'd marry her, probably. That kind of thing."

I whistled then, accidentally, a real note, surprised out of me by the story, and he laughed his whole laugh, the one that started in his shoulders.

That summer we whistled at everything. We whistled at the mail carrier, who whistled back. We whistled at the jays, who did not. We whistled the looping tune in the garden while he showed me how to know when a tomato was ready, which was not by looking but by giving it a gentle squeeze and listening, he claimed, to its answer. I never heard the answer. But I squeezed the tomatoes, and I whistled, and the summer went on.

At the end of August he drove me home. In the driveway he said, "You'll keep it up? The whistling. It's no good if it just sits in a person."

I said I would.

I did, for a while. Then I was ten, and eleven, and it seemed like a kid's trick. I stopped. You stop things without deciding to. The stopping just happens around you, like weather.

He died in October, four years later. I was thirteen. At the funeral my uncle said a few words, and my mother held my hand too hard, and afterward people ate ham in the living room and told stories I had heard before. I went out to the porch. The boards were still the color of driftwood. I pressed my thumb near the railing. The wood still gave a little.

I made a tiny hole. Like a secret about a ladybug. I thought about a bird going over a roof. I thought about a ship at night, and a man whistling into the dark to make sure his brother was still there.

The first note was a bicycle tire. The second was closer. The third was a note, thin and clear, and then another, and then, without planning it, I was whistling the looping tune, the one that had come over the water in the chest of some man I would never meet, through his brother, through my great-great-grandmother, through my grandfather's mouth in a garden, into me.

I don't know if that's how inheritance works. I don't know if a tune is a thing that can be handed down like a ring or a nose or a way of being afraid of heights. But I sat on that porch at thirteen, whistling into the yard where the tomatoes had gone wild and fallen, and I felt sure of one thing, which is that somewhere, in some way I couldn't prove, he could hear it, and it counted.

I still whistle. Not often. In the car, mostly, when a song requires it, or when the kettle is taking too long. But sometimes, for no reason, walking down a street in the evening, I'll send out the looping tune, low, just to the air.

It's no good if it just sits in a person.

And it is a good way to make sure someone's still there.

**Ninety Days**

The lost property office sits at the end of platform zero, past the door marked STAFF ONLY, down a corridor that smells of rain and brake dust. Nell has worked there eleven years. She can date an umbrella by its ribs. Nothing about the job is difficult. Everything about it is strange.

On Tuesday mornings a man named Kofi brings the week's haul in plastic crates: phones without chargers, chargers without phones, a single crutch, a trombone, a hat box containing a wedding veil and nothing else. He reads the found labels in a voice made for radio and never comments on the contents. Nell logs each item in the ledger—date, place, description, a number—and ties on a tag. Then it goes on a shelf to wait.

The waiting is the whole job. Ninety days; that's the rule. Ninety days for someone to retrace their steps, to call, to fill in the form, to stand at the counter with a claim ticket in their fist. Some things go home the same day. Phones especially. A phone is a person's twin, and people arrive for them breathless and apologetic, as if they'd left a child on the train. Umbrellas almost never. Nell has a theory that an umbrella is the only object we buy already intending to abandon it.

What stays past ninety days gets processed. Clothing goes to the charity shop on Mabgate Lane. Devices are wiped. The rest is destroyed, unless a worker wants it, and workers are allowed to want things. In eleven years Nell has taken home a folding chair, a tin of English Breakfast still sealed, a scarf she wears each winter, and a hardback novel with a bus ticket for a bookmark, the journey half finished, someone's plans interrupted at chapter twelve and never resumed.

The things she cannot take home, because they are too much like a person, are the ones that keep her at night. A hearing aid, once, in a yellow case like a tiny coffin. A lunchbox with a child's name on a sticker—Amy Chen, age five by the handwriting—a dent in the lid, a grape gone to raisin in the side compartment. A bunch of keys on a fob shaped like a lemon, labelled in ballpoint, BACK DOOR ONLY. Whose back door? Somewhere there is a house that no longer opens, or opens to strangers, and a person who has had to explain the loss of more than keys.

The wedding dress arrived in March, folded into a dry-cleaner's bag, found on the 18:40 to Sheffield. No hanger, no note. Nell logged it and hung it on the high rail where the coats live, and for ninety days it swung up there among the suitcases like a presence. People came in asking after laptops, briefcases, a guitar. Nobody asked after the dress. On day ninety-one she took it down and stood it on the counter and looked at it a long time. Then she photographed it for the disposal record and did not dispose of it. It is still there. She has decided, privately, against procedure, that some things are not lost. They are left. A left thing is a message. She does not know to whom.

Kofi says send it to the charity shop. His mother was married in a borrowed dress; a dress should be worn. Nell says nothing. There is a version of the story where a woman ran for the train with the dress over her arm and made the train and made the wedding and forgot the bag. There is another version where she sat in carriage C with the bag on her lap the whole way, and at her stop stood and left it on purpose, the way you might leave a stone on a grave.

The counter brings her the living. On Thursdays the office opens to the public and the corridor fills with a queue that is never quite a queue, people leaning on the tiled wall with their stories in their mouths. A woman weeping over a laptop that holds the only photographs of her mother. A man who has come about a saw, and describes it so precisely that Nell, who has seen ten thousand objects and forgotten most of them, could pick it from a hundred others in the dark: eighteen inches, wooden handle, worn smooth on the left side where his thumb went for thirty years. He holds it to his chest when she brings it out. He does not explain the saw. He doesn't have to.

And there is the man who comes every few weeks and claims nothing. He stands at the scarf rail and looks, then thanks her and goes. She asked him once what he was missing. Nothing, he said. Everything's here. I just like to see it. She has stopped asking. The office is a kind of museum if you look at it sideways: a gallery of the moments people dropped.

Last Tuesday Kofi lifted a paper bag out of a crate, a bakery bag, still warm at the seam, two loaves inside, white and seeded, and a receipt for a coffee, black, and a slice of lemon cake, paid by card at 7:12 a.m. Nell logged it: one bag, two loaves. Somewhere on the morning's trains a person was walking around with half a breakfast and a whole morning in their head, late for something, or early, or in love. The loaves went on the shelf. By Friday the bag had gone soft and the office smelled like a kitchen. On day ninety no one had come. The rule says destroy. She kept the lemon-cake receipt. It is in the drawer.

The drawer is under the ledger, and it is the part of the job that does not exist. Single gloves. A cinema ticket. A drawing a child made of a house with too many windows. The lemon keys. Things too small to grieve over and too particular to burn. The ledger would call them unclaimed. The drawer calls them hers. Some nights, locking up, she looks at the shelves—all those coats with their arms hanging, all those cases with nobody's clothes in them—and she thinks that the station above her is a machine for setting people down in the wrong place, and that she works in the organ it uses to remember.

# Lookout

They are retiring me the way they retire a bridge, or a word. Not because I failed. Because I am no longer the cheapest way to do what I do.

Thirty-one summers in this tower. Fourteen feet by fourteen, bolted to a granite shoulder of the range at 7,200 feet. Come October they will replace me with a camera that does not blink, does not dream, does not need a woman to haul water up eighty-one stairs twice a day. The camera will see more, they say. It will never look away.

But looking is not the same as seeing.

I learned that the first summer, from the man I replaced — Hoskie, who had watched this ridge twenty years before me. The mountain would teach me its ordinary, he said. *Watch until the ordinary is worn into you so deep that the smallest change is a shout.*

He was right. It took three seasons. Now I know this forest the way you know a face. I know the fog that pools in Miller Draw like milk in a blue bowl. I know dust raised by the Thursday cattle truck from dust that means something is wrong. I know the bear who crosses the south meadow at dusk is on time, and that when she is late she is usually moving with cubs, and that once — once — she was late because a man stood too still in the trees. That man was a problem I had to call in.

The camera will not know her lateness. It will see a bear. Or it will not. It will file both facts the same.

People think this job is loneliness. They picture a woman going quietly strange among the trees. I have thought about strangeness. I have had time. But loneliness is a word for people with other options on the table. What I have is attention, and attention is not empty. It is a room that fills.

In the mornings the light comes up the valleys like a tide, filling the shadows first, then the meadows, then the high granite, until the basin is a held breath of gold. I have watched that tide four thousand mornings and not tired of it. Tiredness is a failure of particularity. Gold is not gold. It is aspen leaf, and pine resin, and the old fire scar turning amber, and the creek flashing, and my own hands on the railing, lit.

The Osborne Fire Finder sits in the center of the cab, a brass ring on a map of everything I love. I have taken sights on smoke that saved two hundred homes, and sights on nothing — heat shimmer, a green snag steaming after rain — and learned humility. The instrument does not tell you which is which. That is the work.

There was a fire I did not catch. 2012. Dry lightning in the rocks above Bear Wallow, smoldering in a rat's nest of duff where no one could have seen it, though knowing that has never once been any comfort at three in the morning. It grew to eleven thousand acres. It took the Hendersons' place. I had watched their lights come on at dusk for years, a yellow spark in the black, regular as a lighthouse. After the fire there were no lights. I still look for them. The eye does not accept corrections easily.

After that I almost left. Hoskie was gone by then; he'd gone in his sleep the winter before, which is the way a lookout should go if she must. I wrote my resignation on the back of a fire-weather chart and carried it halfway to the truck. Then I stopped. The meadow was doing its evening thing, the bear was late, and I needed to know why. I climbed back up. I stayed eleven more years.

They will say a neural net in Denver can watch a thousand peaks at once, that it does not get cataracts, does not get grief, does not forget. All true. Also true: it will never smell smoke through a screen window at 2 a.m. and know, before any instrument, that it is a slash pile someone lied about putting out. It will not notice that the herons stopped using the north pond this year, or wonder why, or care. Care is not in the spec sheet.

Last night a storm came over Saddleback around ten, walking on its own legs of rain. Lightning hit the ridge three times, close enough that I felt it in my teeth. I marked the strikes, called them in, and sat up with the binoculars until two, listening to the woods tick and settle, the way a house does. Nothing smoked. By morning the sky was rinsed and the bear came across the meadow late again, unhurried, two cubs behind her like punctuation, and I wrote in the log: *All quiet. All seen.*

That is the sentence they will not teach the machine. *All seen.* Not all secure, not all within normal parameters. Seen. The old word. The one that means somebody was here, and stayed, and looked until looking became a form of love.

Friday they come up with a helicopter and a crate. I will carry down what I brought up thirty-one years ago, less a few things given to the mountain. The stairs will seem shorter going down. They always do.

I will not look back from the truck. Lookouts do not look back; it is a professional hazard. I will look once at the Fire Finder's brass ring catching the sun, and then I will drive down into the world of people who no longer have to watch anything longer than a screen.

And somewhere above me a camera will open its dry eye, and the forest will begin teaching it nothing, because a camera cannot be taught, and a forest cannot stop.

I hope it rains. I hope the bear is on time. I hope, when the next dry lightning walks the ridge, that whatever watches then will have wanted, all those years, to be there.

**The Unsent**

We found them on the third day of clearing the house, in the bottom drawer of the rolltop desk, under a manual and a dead flashlight. A copy-paper box, the free kind, filled with envelopes. My sister pulled one out, read the front, handed it to me, and went on sorting.

My name, in his handwriting — the careful print he'd used on my lunch bags and my permission slips and, once, on the sign at my wedding: RESERVED. Every envelope was addressed to me. Every one had a stamp. Not one had been mailed.

There were a hundred and forty-six of them. We counted twice.

The earliest was dated June 4, 1981. I was four. The latest was dated the Tuesday before he died, eleven weeks ago. The stamps were wrong on half of them — too little postage, out-of-date rates — so he never checked. He wrote them knowing they would not go anywhere. He wrote them the way you talk into a pillow.

I took the box home. I told my sister I'd catalog them. I did not catalog them. I read them out of order, in the evenings, and then I started over and read them in order, and I will tell you some of what they said, because I have decided they were not private. Private is a word for things you're ashamed of. These were something else.

June 4, 1981: "You had a fever of 102 and I sat up with you and you asked me if the stars were hot. I said yes. You said, good, and went to sleep. I stayed up. I didn't know yet that I would keep staying up."

That's the fourth one. The first one is shorter. It says: "I am going to write these and not send them. I read about a man who did that. I don't remember where. It seemed useful."

A man in a magazine. That was the whole origin. My father, who did not finish college, who read the paper back to front and the manuals first, read about unsent letters in a magazine and started a thirty-eight-year correspondence with his daughter, postage due.

There is a letter for every B I cried over — he was not disappointed, he was terrified, there is a difference, he should have said so. There is a letter for the night I left for college, when he followed the car to the end of the driveway and then went inside and washed the car. "I washed a car that was already clean," he wrote. "Your mother pretended not to notice. She was good at that. I married her for it."

There is a letter about my wedding that I will not summarize except to say that he liked my husband more than he ever let on, and worried about him too, the way you worry about a boat you have watched leave the harbor.

There is a letter about the dog. There is a letter about the fight we had when I was thirty — I don't remember the fight, but he remembered it, he remembered my exact words, he had been carrying them. There is a letter that is only a recipe, for the chicken thing, the one I asked for at the hospital once and he said he'd write it down and never did. He wrote it down. He drew a diagram of the pan.

The handwriting changes in 1997. It gets smaller, tighter. He never told us about the tremor. There is a letter about the tremor.

The last ones are short. In March he wrote about the birds at the feeder, the finches that came in a pack of twelve, and how he had started naming them, all the same name. In April he wrote: "I am not afraid, exactly. I am annoyed. There is a difference. You taught me the difference, though you didn't mean to, when you were four and the stars were hot."

The last letter is dated the Tuesday before he died. It says: "Don't worry. I didn't send this. I never sent any of them. I want you to know that I knew what I was doing. I wasn't hiding. I was keeping. There is a difference, and I should have said so."

There is a difference, and he should have said so. That could be the epitaph. I have half a mind to put it on the stone.

Here is what I know now, or believe, which in my family is the same tense. Some people love out loud, and some people love in a copy-paper box at the bottom of a desk, and you don't get to choose which one you get, and you don't get to choose which one you are. He was not a man who talked into pillows. I take that back. He was a man who talked into a pillow for thirty-eight years and then labeled the pillow with my name and a stamp he never licked.

My sister thinks I should have them published. She thinks there is a book in them, a universal father. I told her no. Some correspondence is not for an audience. Some letters do their work by existing, the way a bridge does its work even when no one is on it.

But I did one thing. I took a legal pad — he would have liked that, the yellow, the lines — and I wrote him back. I told him about the finches at my own feeder, twelve of them, or maybe the same one twelve times. I told him the stars are hot, and that I stayed up. I told him about the chicken thing, that I made it, that the pan was wrong but it was close.

I addressed it to him. I put a stamp on it. I did not mail it. I put it in the box with the others, on top, the newest letter, the first reply.

It seemed useful.

**Machine Six**

The dryers at the Sunbeam sound like a train that never arrives. That's what I thought my first night, back when I still had the energy for metaphors. Now I mostly think in quarters. Quarters for the wash, quarters for the dry, quarters for the candy machine that takes your money and gives you nothing, which is its own kind of honesty.

I work eleven to seven, five nights a week. Three years now. People think a laundromat at 3 a.m. would be empty, but the city at that hour is a different country, and its citizens are insomniacs, nurses, cabdrivers, and people who have run out of other places to be. One fluorescent tube buzzes like it's clearing its throat to speak, then deciding against it. There's a bulletin board with a flyer for a missing cat named Duchess, dated 2019. The cat is definitely gone. The flyer stays. At the Sunbeam we understand about waiting.

The regulars come in a rotation, like weather. Tuesdays it's Priya, who works labor and delivery and sometimes sits with her eyes closed while her scrubs go around, still carrying that hospital smell, which is clean and terrible at once. She never sleeps in the chair. She says if she sleeps she'll miss the spin cycle, and the spin cycle is the closest thing she gets to a conclusion. Thursdays, two brothers bring garbage bags of clothes from their mother's house — she moved to assisted living in October — and they fight quietly about which of them their mother likes less. It's closer than you'd think. Fridays a kid named Marcus washes his basketball uniform at midnight over a superstition involving free throws, and I have learned not to argue with a man and his free throws.

And then there's the old man.

He comes in around two, Sundays, when the place is at its emptiest. He is tall the way old tall men are, stooped like a question mark that has given up on the answer. He uses machine six, the one by the window, and he washes a single pillowcase. White cotton, gone soft gray at the fold. No other clothes. He sits with his hands on his knees for the forty minutes the machine runs, watching it like television. Then he takes the pillowcase out, folds it into a neat square, puts it inside his coat, and leaves. He has never once used a dryer. Whatever he is drying, he dries it at home, or he dries it nowhere.

I have had three years to ask him about it. I never have. There's a rule I made without deciding to: you don't ask the night people why. Night is where people bring the things that can't sit in the daylight laundromat of their lives, the things that would look like nothing in the morning — a pillowcase, a bag of a dead mother's blouses, a uniform that has to be washed at midnight or the free throws will know. You don't go pawing through that. The machines do the washing. That's already more intimacy than most of us can stand.

Last winter I learned his name by accident. The dry cleaner next door, Mrs. Bao, was shoveling the sidewalk, and he stopped to take the shovel from her and finish the job, and she called him Mr. Ander. Just that. Mr. Ander, thank you, Mr. Ander, go inside before you fall. He nodded at me like we were strangers, which technically we were, and which by then we were not.

In February I tore my meniscus on the ice outside and sat in the office with it raised on a milk crate, and I heard machine six start without looking. When I came out to change the bathroom sign, he was sitting forward, and the pillowcase — I couldn't help seeing — had a tear in it, a long one, like it had given up a seam. He held the folded square in his lap when the cycle ended, and he sat with it a while, the way you sit with a decision.

The next Sunday the tear was mended. Badly. Someone had sewn it up with thread that didn't match, big blobs of stitches, the kind of sewing that is really just apologizing to a thing for not letting it go. My grandmother mended everything twice, once for strength and once for looks, and she said the second mending was for God. Mr. Ander's mending was the first kind only.

In March he brought a second pillowcase. Same white cotton, same gray fold, but a different case — I could tell because the first one had a small brown stain near the seam that I had stopped pretending not to notice. He washed them both. He sat with his hands on his knees. He folded them both into squares, put them both inside his coat, and left, and I understood that something had happened, though I couldn't have said what. A drawer emptied, maybe. A decision about a bed. The second pillowcase arriving the way a second truth arrives: quietly, after the first one has been carried alone for years.

He stopped coming in April.

I want to tell you I asked Mrs. Bao, that I found an obituary, that I learned the whole story — the wife, the bed, the years. I didn't. I want to tell you I kept his pillowcase, that it's in a drawer. It isn't. What I have is machine six, which I still run empty some Sunday nights around two, when the place is at its emptiest — a quarter in the slot, forty minutes of water going around for no one. The other attendants think I'm testing it. Let them.

The dryers still sound like a train that never arrives. I know now that the point of a train sound is not the arriving. It's that while it sounds, you are somewhere, and something of yours is turning, getting cleaner, getting ready to be folded into a square and carried home.

**Gelatin Silver**

The photograph arrives on a Tuesday, in a manila envelope that has been opened and resealed so many times the flap has gone soft as cloth. Inside, wrapped in a page of the *Guardian* dated four years ago, is a picture of a woman on a beach.

Marta lifts it out with cotton gloves. She has been restoring photographs for twenty-six years, and she can tell the story of a print before anyone speaks. This one is a gelatin silver print, mid-century, hand-finished — someone has tinted the woman's lips a faint rose. It has been folded once, through the face. It has been wet, once, and dried badly, so the emulsion has a tide line across the sky. Along the edges, the silver has begun to migrate to the surface, a bluish metallic sheen like light on the back of a fish.

The man who brought it — Mr. Halloran, eighty-one, hat held at his chest like he is in a church — says only: "It's my wife. We were in Bournemouth. I'd like her face back, if you can."

He does not say that his wife is dead. He does not need to. They all bring the dead in manila envelopes.

Marta scans the photograph at a thousand dots per inch, and the woman appears on the monitor in a size no camera in 1958 could have promised her. This is the moment Marta loves and does not love. At this magnification a photograph stops being a picture and becomes a landscape. She can see the grain of the paper, the individual silver particles like a sky of fine sand. She can see where the fold has taken the woman's left eye and turned it into a white seam. She can see that the tinting hand — some studio worker in Bournemouth, paid by the print — gave the woman's cheeks a little color but left her hands the gray of the shingle behind her.

She begins, as she always begins, with the damage. She works in layers, building the repair the way the original print was built: dark first, then midtone, then light. A photograph, she is fond of telling the apprentices who last a season, is not a thing. It is an arrangement of light that agreed to stay. The woman on the beach is not a woman. She is a cheekbone that caught the sun, an eye socket that held the shadow of a brow, a chin that sent a small bright signal downward into the gray of a collar. Restore the light and you restore the woman. Disturb it and you have a stranger.

The fold through the eye is the worst of it. Marta works an hour on the left eye alone, pulling tone from the undamaged right and mirroring it, then breaking the symmetry, because a face is never its own reflection. An eye is not white with a dark dot. It is a wet stone in a setting of small muscles, and the light sits on it differently depending on whether the person is looking at the sun or away from it.

This woman is looking slightly off-camera. Marta notices it around three o'clock, when she leans back from the screen and lets the face come together at viewing distance. The woman is not posing. Or she is posing, but something has happened — a gull, a remark, the photographer himself doing something foolish to fix her expression — and the pose has broken open into attention. Her eyes have the crinkle of a laugh that has not quite arrived. Her mouth is closed around a smile she is saving.

Marta has restored eleven hundred faces. She has seen the dead look at the camera, look past the camera, look through it. She has seen people hold themselves so stiffly that the photograph feels like a held breath. She has rarely seen a face so clearly aimed at someone who is not in the picture.

She works until seven. She repairs the tide line in the sky, the silvering at the borders, the seam through the eye. She does not touch the lips' faint rose. Studio tinting is a period fact, like the shape of the sunglasses on the rock beside the woman, and Marta is a restorer, not a revisionist. She is not there to improve the past. She is there to make it visible again.

On Thursday, Mr. Halloran comes to collect it. She has made two prints: one on fiber paper, processed to archival standard, and a smaller one, which she does not explain. He sits in the chair she offers and takes the larger print in both hands, and he does not speak for a long time. Marta has learned not to fill these silences. Whatever is happening is not happening in the room.

"That's not how she looked," he says finally.

Marta's stomach does the small drop it does. *The eye is wrong. The mouth. I've made her a stranger.*

"That's how she looked at me," he says.

He is looking at the off-camera place the woman is looking. He has not needed the fold repaired to know what was there. He has had the original in drawers and envelopes and the backs of other photographs for sixty-six years, and he has known, the whole time, where the missing person in the picture is standing. He is standing where Mr. Halloran is sitting now.

He takes the smaller print, the one she made without explaining, and he understands it immediately, which is how she knows she was right to make it. It is a crop: just the woman's face, just the expression, the laugh that had not arrived. "This is the one that goes on the mantel," he says. "The other is the one that's ours."

After he leaves, Marta sits in the gray afternoon light of her studio and looks at the scan still open on the monitor, the woman at a thousand dots per inch, a country made of silver. It occurs to her, not for the first time, that a photograph never holds a person. It holds a few grams of light that bounced off a person on one afternoon and agreed, for a moment, to stay. Everything else — the laugh, the marriage, the death, the man in the hat — is inference. We look at a beach in 1958 and we see a whole life, because we cannot help it, because the light will not stay unless we do this, because a face looking slightly off-camera is an invitation, and someone must accept it.

She closes the file. Outside, the light is doing what it always does — arriving, touching everything, leaving. Somewhere it is bouncing off a cheekbone right now, on its way to a negative that has not yet been made. She hopes someone will be kind to it. She hopes someone will understand that the face is not the face. The face is how it looked at you.

# One Word a Page

The dictionary cost a dollar at the estate sale, wedged between a bread machine nobody wanted and a box of Christmas candles. Webster's Collegiate, ninth edition, spine cracked to white. I bought it because my old dictionary had drowned in a basement flood and I had been making do with the internet, which hands you a word the way a vending machine hands you a candy bar — instantly, and without any sense that a word has neighbors, or a history, or a body.

It wasn't until I got home that I found the underlines.

Someone had gone through this dictionary the way a child goes through a coloring book. On the first page, a clean stroke beneath *abandon*. On the second, *abate*. Not every page. Not random pages either, or so it seemed at first. One word, sometimes two, then a stretch of ten or fifty pages in silence. I sat on the floor in the window light and turned the pages like a person dealing out a fortune.

*Abandon. Abate. Aberrant. Abide.*

I want to tell you I didn't make a list. I made a list.

The sale had been for a house on Maple Street, the kind with a screened porch and a flag holder by the door. The woman running the cash box said the owner had lived there forty years. A teacher, maybe. A widow. She didn't know much. "She kept to herself," the woman said, which is what people say when they mean they never asked.

From the A's I copied: *after, alone, amber, anchor, answer, archipelago, attend, August, awake.*

I looked the sale up that night and found the obituary. Her name was Ruth Voss. Born 1931. Taught fourth grade for thirty-one years. Husband dead in 1988. Garden, church, a nephew in Ohio. The obituary did not mention words. Most obituaries don't. They list the weather of a life without ever saying what fell.

The B's: *because, begin, believe, beneath, bird, bloom, breathe, bright.* The C's: *candle, carry, certain, chase, clear, close, cloud, come.* I noticed the words leaning one direction — verbs of continuing, nouns of weather and light. A person could live inside a list like that. A person could be trying to.

I started writing a story about her. In my story she left a marriage in 1974 and drove to the ocean with a dictionary on the passenger seat. I gave her a blue coat. Then I realized I had given her my blue coat, and I stopped writing the story. That is the trouble with any trace of a stranger. You read it like a mirror and call it a biography.

A friend of mine said, people underline in books, old people especially, it doesn't mean a thing. Maybe she just liked the drag of the pen. But the lines were confident — one stroke, no going back over, the ballpoint never hesitating on the fiber. And it was the same pen the whole way through, blue, until the last quarter of the book, where the ink goes black and the lines begin to wobble. The hand was older. Or tired. Or both.

I tried to imagine the nights. A kitchen table. A lamp with a pull chain. She would not have been reading for information — you don't read a dictionary for information. You read it the way you walk a property line, to see what's yours, to see what holds. Maybe it was a game she played with a grandchild who didn't exist. Maybe it was prayer. Some people close their eyes and put a finger on a page and believe the finger is guided. The underlines were too many for that, and too patient. This was not one answer sought. This was a practice.

You cannot hurry a book you've promised to meet one word at a time. That is the opposite of skimming. Skimming is how we read now, and I don't except myself. We take the vending-machine word and go. She had chosen the other thing: the whole field of the page, and one word allowed to survive it. Every page a small field. Every underline a decision about what matters. It must have changed her. A discipline like that always does. It's the grandmother shelling peas on the porch — the point was never the peas.

In the S's the wobbling got worse. *Stay. Still. Sure.* Then a long pause — forty pages of nothing — and then, in a black, uncertain line, *remain.*

The T's: *tender, threshold, tonight, trace, true.* The W's: *wait, want, weather, window.* Then almost nothing. The X's and Y's went by clean. On the last page of the dictionary, among the z's — *zeal, zenith, zinc, zither, zone* — no mark at all.

The last underlined word, two pages earlier, was *again.*

I sat with that for a while. *Again* is a word that only works if there is a next time. It is a word that does not close a book. She could have underlined *end.* She owned the pen. She chose *again.*

I started my own underlining around the G's. Not to imitate her. All right — to imitate her. It changed the reading within a week. I slowed down. I began to see pages as fields instead of corridors. I began to fail at it, too — to underline three words, then four, then to catch myself hoarding, and to put the pen down. One word a page is a fast way to find out what you actually want. Most of us want everything. She didn't. Or she trained herself not to.

I don't know what I'll do at the last page. Leave it clean, probably. Some words should arrive unchosen, the way mornings do.

But I copied her list out fair, all of it, and pinned it above my desk, and I will tell you the strangest thing. I cannot read it as hers anymore. I read it and it is my voice saying the words. *After, alone, amber, again.* Whatever she was doing at that kitchen table for all those years, it worked. The words got out.

**Seven**

I name colours for a living. Not colours that exist — those already have names, most of them stolen from birds and metals and the sea — but colours that don't exist yet, which is to say colours that already exist as something else and are waiting for a wall.

The company calls me a Colour Stylist. On my business cards, which I have never given anyone, it says Colour & Trend Manager. What I do is mix small cups of paint and look at them under different lights and wait for a word to arrive. Moorhen. Held Breath. Last Orders. Waiting Room. First Frost, Late. Wrong Weather. You cannot rush it. A name that is only a description is a failure. A name that is only a mood is a lie. You want the place where the two meet.

The new collection is yellows. The brief says: optimistic, domestic, new morning; nothing too egg, nothing too mustard, nothing that reminds anyone of a hospital corridor. I have made fourteen yellows in two weeks and hated all of them. They were too clean. Yellows are the hardest. Everyone has a yellow in them somewhere, and it is never paint.

My mother's kitchen was yellow. Not decor yellow. It had started as something braver, a mustard the man in the shop had sworn was Buttermilk, and twenty years of sun through the east window and steam off the kettle and the oven door left open had worked on it, cured it, the way a river cures a stone. By the end it was a yellow that had given up towards green at the edges. A yellow like the inside of a lemon leaf, like light through a cider bottle, like a page of old sheet music. In photographs it looks sick. In life, at seven in the morning, with my mother at the stove and the radio doing its low talking and the window cracked to the garden even in November, it was the exact colour of being safe.

I have a chip of that wall. I took it the last time I was in the house, before the buyers painted everything in a white they call Bright Cloud, which is the colour of nothing. The chip lives in my desk drawer with eleven years of rejected swatches, and some evenings I hold it to the window and try to be professional about it.

I mixed fourteen yellows and none of them were it. Cream and raw umber, a hook of green, a breath of grey — too intentional, all of them. The original was an accident. It was made by time and steam and a woman who opened the window because she liked the cold on her wrists while she waited for the kettle. You cannot specify that in a formula. I sent the company fourteen yellows that were merely yellow, and they chose one called New Day, which is the colour of a corridor, and I said nothing, because I was brought up not to make a fuss.

Then in March I let myself into the empty house — I was in the town for a funeral, someone else's — and stood in the kitchen, Bright Cloud now, and held my chip to the wall, and understood, at last, professionally, what I had been failing to match. The colour was never on the wall. The colour was seven in the morning. It was the light coming through the east window at the angle that only exists in autumn and early spring, through a garden that needed weeding, into a room that smelled of coffee and dish soap and the particular cold of a window left open, and my mother in the middle of it, stirring something, saying, There's bread if you want toast. Take the colour away from the morning and the woman, and it is only a sickly yellow-green, as the photographs correctly report.

I came home and mixed a fifteenth yellow. I did it with my eyes almost shut, not being a professional. Cream, a little ochre, a little green, a little grey, and then — this is the part I will not put in the report — I opened the window and let the cold in on my wrists and added one more drop of green. For the garden.

I named it Seven.

The company changed it, of course. Marketing said Seven was a number, a loner, a hospital ward. They wanted lifestyle. They launched it as Morning Kitchen, and it sold better than anything in the collection. I see it now in places I never expected: a nursery in a magazine, a café in Leeds, the waiting room of a dentist I went to for a chipped tooth. A whole wall of it, parents and children and the radio doing its low talking. Strangers eating their breakfast in my mother's kitchen light.

I thought this would be unbearable. It is not unbearable. It is a different thing. It turns out you can put a person in a can if you try. Not the whole person — not the hands, or the voice, or the way she said my name when I came in from the cold — but the colour of the morning she made, which was the person, as near as paint can come. People carry her home by the handle. They brush her onto their mornings. They wipe their children's porridge off her and never learn her name, and in the trade I still call it Seven, quietly, under my breath, the way you speak to the dead so they won't feel left out.

Somewhere it is always seven in the morning. Somewhere the window is open and the kettle is taking its time and a woman is stirring something and saying there's bread if you want toast. I did that. I put her in gallons. I gave her away one wall at a time, and if that is not what paint is for, I don't know what it is for.

**The Tuning**

The appointment book said: Mrs. Okonkwo, 3 p.m., upright, not played in years. That last part is what I look for. A piano that is played every day goes out of tune slowly, almost politely. A piano that sits—those are the ones with opinions.

I found the house at the end of a street that dead-ended into a conservation area. Birch trees. A mailbox leaning like it had given up arguing with the wind. Mrs. Okonkwo was already at the door. She was small, maybe eighty, wearing a cardigan the color of weak tea, and she looked at my case the way people look at a doctor's bag: with hope and dread in the same expression.

"It was my husband's," she said, before I had even taken off my coat. "He tuned it himself. He thought nobody else would do it properly."

In the front room stood a 1962 Zender upright, walnut case, the kind of piano that was built to survive a flood. It had been beautiful once. Now the ivory had gone the color of old teeth, and someone—him, I supposed—had drawn a small pencil star on middle C, years ago, the way children mark a territory.

I opened the lid. Inside, the felt was intact, the strings not yet eaten by rust, but the pitch had fallen. They always fall. A piano is a tension structure, thirty-odd tons of pull across a cast-iron plate, and the world is always trying to flatten it. Humidity, gravity, time. Silence is not rest for a piano. Silence is just another kind of weather.

I put the mute strips in and started with the temperament, middle of the keyboard, the way my teacher taught me: listen for the beating, the wobble between two strings that should be one. When a unison is out, you hear it as a kind of tremor, a slow shiver in the note. You turn the pin until the shiver dies. Then the octave. Then the fifth, which you flatten a hair, because a perfect fifth is too pure for human ears—we like them slightly compromised.

It took about twenty minutes before she spoke again.

"I haven't opened that piano since he died."

I said that was all right. I didn't say that pianos can go so flat that raising them in one pass will snap strings. I didn't say that some pianos are past it, that I sometimes recommend people buy a keyboard and be done with the whole business. Her piano wasn't past it. I could tell from the first note that under the neglect there was still a center, a true note hiding inside the sour one. You don't find that in every instrument. You don't find it in every person, either, but I try not to say things like that out loud.

She told me he had been a schoolteacher. Music, then science, then whatever they needed. He built a telescope from a cardboard tube and a kit. He tuned the piano on the first of every month, she said, whether it needed it or not. She used to sit on the sofa and read while he worked, and she could tell from the sound whether it was going to be a good month or a hard one—the months when the piano was far gone, when he had to lean into the pins, go quiet with concentration.

"I thought I'd want it gone," she said. "I gave away his coat. I gave away his chair. Then I got to the piano and I couldn't. I thought, someone will come and take it, eventually."

*Eventually* had lasted four years.

I worked. She made tea I didn't drink. The light in the room went from afternoon to the beginning of evening without either of us turning on a lamp, and I kept tuning, string by string, until the unisons stopped shivering and the octaves locked and the whole instrument, which had begun the day as a cupboard full of sadness, started to sound like a piano again.

That's the part of the job I can't explain to people who ask why I still do it. Not the money. The moment when an instrument that has been dead comes back—not new, never new, but itself. The old Zender had a bright voice, a little nasal, honest. The kind of piano that would never flatter you. You played a wrong note on that instrument and it would tell you. I thought her husband had chosen well.

When I finished, I closed the lid, put my tools away, and she sat down on the bench. Her hands went to middle C—the one with the star—and she played a scale. Slowly. Then a chord. Then, after a moment, the beginning of something I didn't recognize, a hymn or a folk song, the kind of tune that lives in the fingers even when the person insists they've forgotten how to play.

She stopped after eight bars. Her back was to me. I looked at the bookshelf and gave her that, at least.

"He tuned it on the first of the month," she said. "I thought that was a bit obsessive."

"Monthly is sensible, for an upright in this climate."

"No," she said. "I think he just liked the sitting with it. The being alone with it, with the lid open. I used to think he was working. I think now he was praying."

I didn't have anything to say to that, so I said something about booking the next tuning for six weeks, and she wrote the date on the calendar by the telephone, the paper calendar people still use when they have outlived their phones' usefulness. I carried my case to the car. The birches had gone gold at the edges. The streetlight came on with a small electric sigh.

I think about that piano sometimes. How it sat for four years, going flat, holding its husband-shaped silence, waiting for someone to put their hands on it and find out it still had a center. Most of us are not so lucky. Most of us go out of tune in public, in company, slowly enough that nobody hears the beating, the tremor in the unison, and no one comes with a lever and a mute strip and the patience to listen for the true note underneath.

I should call more people back. I should sit with more pianos. I wrote the next appointment in my book—Mrs. Okonkwo, six weeks—and under the date I put a small star. Middle C. The way he would have.

# Unclaimed

The office of the transit lost and found is a long room under the station, lit by fluorescents that hum at a frequency just below a headache. I have worked here eleven years. People imagine I spend my days returning things, and sometimes I do. A woman's face when she sees her grandmother's scarf folded in tissue paper is a sight I will never tire of. But most of what arrives is never claimed.

There is a shelf for umbrellas — hundreds, black and plaid, and one shaped like a parrot. There is a cabinet for electronics, a drawer for keys, a bin for single gloves. There is a locked case for things of obvious value and a box for things of no value that someone might still want: a child's drawing of a horse, a grocery list, a funeral program with a photograph of a man mid-laugh.

Unclaimed things stay with me ninety days. Then they are catalogued, boxed, and sent to a warehouse, and eventually most are destroyed or given away. I am the last person who will ever look at them carefully.

A wedding dress came in once, found on the 11:15, still in its garment bag, a dry cleaner's ticket pinned to the hanger. We called the cleaner. No record. We posted a description. Nobody came. For three months the dress hung on the back of my door, and every morning I looked at it and wondered whether the wedding had happened, whether this was a spare, whether someone had run. I dry-cleaned it myself, at my own expense, so it would not yellow while it waited.

A man's whole life arrived in a suitcase once: photographs, letters tied with ribbon, a marriage certificate, a discharge paper. We traced the name. He had died the year before, in another city. His nephew had carried the suitcase onto the train and left it on the luggage rack and walked away. When we called, the nephew said, in a voice I still hear, "I don't want it. I took it so the landlords wouldn't throw it out, but I don't have room, and I didn't really know him." The suitcase sat beside my desk for a long time. I read the letters. I shouldn't have, but I did. He wrote to his wife in 1963: "The city is loud, but you are in it, so it is home." She was in the photographs. They had no children. The suitcase is in a warehouse now, in a box marked miscellaneous, which is the truest word I know.

People ask whether I take things home. Officially, no. There is a rule. But last winter a coat came in — a woman's wool coat, navy, hole in the pocket — and in the pocket a theater stub and a hair clip shaped like a star. I waited the ninety days. I called the theater. The show had closed. I looked at that coat every day and thought about my mother, dead six years now, whose coats I gave away too fast, in that first brutal month when you want nothing in the house that still holds a shape.

I took the clip. Only the clip. It sits on my desk, and when the light catches it, it throws a small star onto the ceiling that I am probably the only person who has ever noticed.

What have I learned from eleven years of other people's forgotten things? That people write their names in books and then lose the books. That the thing you grab on the way out the door is never the thing you lose. That grief makes people leave objects on trains — I cannot count the urns, the folded flags, the hospital bracelets that have passed through this room. That almost everyone who loses a phone calls it immediately from a borrowed one, and you can hear the relief in the ring. That people lose the same umbrella twice and are embarrassed both times, and I pretend not to remember.

And that most of what we carry is replaceable, and the rest is not, and you cannot tell which is which by looking.

Last month a boy came in, nineteen maybe, looking for a backpack. It wasn't there. He stood in the doorway a long time, then said, "It had my brother's hoodie in it." I knew before he said anything else that the brother was dead. You learn the grammar. I searched the warehouse records. I called three depots. Nothing.

He said, "It was just a hoodie." He said it the way people do, to make it smaller. I gave him numbers for the other terminals and a card with my name, and I told him things surface. Sometimes they do. Six weeks later a backpack matching his description came in off a bus, and I called him, and he arrived before I had finished hanging up. He put the hoodie on right there, over his clothes, and stood a moment with his eyes closed.

I don't always get that. Mostly I get the dress on the door, the suitcase in the warehouse, the parrot umbrella nobody will ever want and that I cannot bring myself to discard.

At the end of my shift I turn off the lights. The room goes dark except for the exit sign and, if the streetlight is at the right angle, the small star from the clip. I stand a moment in the dark with all of it — the gloves, the phones, the unclaimed photographs of strangers' dogs — and then I go home, taking nothing, or almost nothing, with me.

People think the job is about objects. It is not. It is about the moment after the doors close, that half-second when a person realizes, and puts a hand flat on the glass. I collect what is on the other side of the glass. I keep it safe. I wait.

Most of them do not come back. The waiting is the job. The waiting is the whole of it.
